populations.name: Neandertals
populations.description: An archaic human group of western Eurasia, known from fossils and from several high-quality genomes. Their DNA survives in all present-day people whose ancestry lies largely outside Africa.
populations.genetic_profile: Sampled genomes range from the Altai Mountains to western Europe. The Neandertals who contributed DNA to modern humans were closer to the western (Vindija, Mezmaiskaya) Neandertals than to the Altai individual.

membership.notes: AADR labels ending in _Neanderthal. Excludes the Neandertal–Denisovan first-generation offspring (Russia_Denisova_Neanderthal_Mix).

caveats: Most sampled Neandertal genomes predate the V1 window; only a few late individuals (about 50,000–40,000 years ago) fall inside it.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Neandertals were an archaic human group of western Eurasia known from fossils and from several high-quality genomes. The genomes come from Denisova Cave in the Altai (Siberia), Vindija Cave in Croatia and Mezmaiskaya in the Caucasus. The Vindija woman lived about 50,000 years ago, and the Altai woman roughly 122,000 years ago. Most sampled Neandertals therefore predate the V1 window.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Neandertal populations were small: the Vindija woman has fewer differences between her two genome copies than present-day people. The Altai woman's parents were related at about half-sibling level. The Neandertals who mixed with modern humans were closer to the Vindija and Mezmaiskaya individuals than to the Altai individual.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Neandertal DNA survives in all present-day people whose ancestry lies largely outside Africa, at 1.5-2.1% by one estimate. Most of it traces to one extended period of gene flow 50,500-43,500 years ago. The earliest modern humans in Europe, at Bacho Kiro and Oase, had Neandertal ancestors only a few generations back.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Neandertals who actually mixed with modern humans are not sampled; the genomes are relatives of them. Studies disagree on whether Neandertal ancestry fell over time in European hunter-gatherers: one finds a drop from 3-6% to about 2%, a later study does not. Genome-based ages are tentative.

populations.name: Denisovans
populations.description: An archaic human group known mainly from genomes recovered at Denisova Cave in the Altai. Denisovan-related DNA survives at the highest levels in people of Oceania and parts of Island Southeast Asia.
populations.genetic_profile: Related to Neandertals. The Denisovans who contributed DNA to modern humans were only distantly related to the sampled Altai individual; at least two differently related Denisovan sources are detected in present-day East Asians.

region.name: Known from the Altai (Denisova Cave); inferred elsewhere in Asia

membership.notes: Only the genetically Denisovan individuals. Russia_DenisovaCave (a ~24,000-year-old modern human from the same cave) is deliberately excluded.

caveats: All sampled Denisovan genomes predate the V1 window; the populations that admixed with modern humans are unsampled and their locations unknown.
AADR also has a modern human from Denisova Cave; a site is not a population.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Denisovans were an archaic human group known mainly from genomes recovered at Denisova Cave in the Altai. A finger bone first yielded the genome of a group related to Neandertals, and a tooth carries a very similar mitochondrial genome. They are named after the cave, and shared a common origin with Neandertals. Their genomes come from a small number of bones in that one cave.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Denisovans are related to Neandertals, and at least 0.5% of the Denisovan genome comes from Neandertal gene flow. There is also evidence of gene flow into Denisovans from an unknown archaic group. The Denisovan sources that mixed with modern humans differ in how closely they resemble the sampled Altai individual.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Denisovan-related DNA survives at the highest levels in people of Oceania and parts of Island Southeast Asia. In East Asians, Denisovan segments fall into two components, indicating at least two Denisovan-related sources. Ayta Magbukon of the Philippines carry about 30-40% more Denisovan ancestry than Australians and Papuans, consistent with a separate admixture event.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: All sampled Denisovan genomes predate the V1 window, and the groups that mixed with modern humans are unsampled and their locations unknown. The number of Denisovan sources and the timing of each mixing are inferred from present-day genomes. The Altai individual is not itself shown to be the source population.

populations.name: Shared ancestors of non-Africans (inferred)
populations.description: A modelled population: the common ancestors of nearly all present-day people whose ancestry lies largely outside Africa, who received Neandertal gene flow before dispersing. No individual from it has been sampled and its location is unknown.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: The time range shown is the window of the shared Neandertal gene flow (50,500–43,500 years ago, Iasi et al. 2024), not the population's lifespan.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This is a modelled population, not a sampled one: the shared ancestors of nearly all present-day people whose ancestry lies largely outside Africa. They received Neandertal gene flow before dispersing. No individual from it has been sampled and its location is unknown. The dates on the timeline show the window of the shared gene flow, not how long the population lived.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: The main Neandertal gene flow into this population is dated 50,500-43,500 years ago in one analysis and 45,000-49,000 years ago in another, anchored by a 45,000-year-old genome. Earlier estimates from present-day genomes were wider: 37,000-86,000 years ago. Genetics does not say where the mixing took place.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Present-day non-Africans carry about 1.5-2.6% Neandertal ancestry, depending on the reference genome and method. Most of it traces to a single extended period of gene flow. Early modern humans such as Ust'-Ishim, Oase 1 and the Bacho Kiro individuals show extra, more recent Neandertal ancestors. Some older individuals outside Africa belong to other, different populations.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Dates for the mixing vary from about 37,000 to 86,000 years ago and from 7,000-13,000 years before Ust'-Ishim lived, depending on method. The population is a model and no one from it is sampled. Whether East Asians had a second pulse is not settled; two ancient genomes fit a single one.

populations.name: Zlatý kůň/Ranis population
populations.description: A small population of early modern humans known from two sites in central Europe, about 45,000 years ago. The individuals were closely related to each other, even across sites.
populations.genetic_profile: The earliest split from the out-of-Africa population sampled so far. No detectable continuity with later Europeans.
populations.archaeological_context: The Ranis remains are associated with the Lincombian–Ranisian–Jerzmanowician (LRJ) assemblage.

membership.notes: All Ranis and Zlatý kůň individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are early modern humans from two sites in central Europe, Ranis (Ilsenhohle Cave, Germany) and Zlaty kun (Czechia), who lived about 45,000 years ago. The 2024 study identified six individuals at Ranis, including a mother and her young daughter, and linked them to the Zlaty kun skull through distant family ties. They belong to one small, closely related population.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Zlaty kun/Ranis population is the deepest known split from the Out-of-Africa lineage: it separated earlier than the lineages leading to Bacho Kiro and Ust'-Ishim. Its Neandertal ancestry comes from the admixture shared by all non-Africans, dated 45,000-49,000 years ago. Two Ranis males carry Y haplogroup NO, like Ust'-Ishim.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The population shows no detectable continuity with later Europeans: it did not contribute ancestry to later hunter-gatherers. It is the earliest sampled branch of the population that left Africa and received Neandertal gene flow. Its effective size was small, about 300, and its members show long stretches of homozygosity.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Zlaty kun skull could not be dated directly, so its age comes from kinship and Neandertal segment length. One paper reports a possible Zlaty kun contribution to Crimean Buran Kaya III individuals, which this study could not reproduce. Population size estimates come from genetic models.

populations.name: Bacho Kiro IUP-associated individuals
populations.description: Individuals from Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, about 46,000–43,000 years ago, buried with an Initial Upper Palaeolithic stone-tool assemblage. All had Neandertal ancestors only a few generations back.
populations.genetic_profile: More closely related to later East Asians and Native Americans than to later western Eurasians.

membership.notes: IUP layers only; the later Bacho Kiro UP individual is not included.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are individuals from Bacho Kiro Cave in Bulgaria, dated about 45,930-42,580 years ago, found with an Initial Upper Palaeolithic stone tool assemblage. They are the earliest Late Pleistocene modern humans recovered in Europe so far. The label groups three people by archaeological context; a later individual from the same cave (BK1653, about 35,000 years old) is not included.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The three individuals are more closely related to later East Asians and Native Americans than to later western Eurasians. In admixture graphs they relate to populations that contributed to Tianyuan. Each carried 3.0-3.8% Neandertal DNA, more than most humans, and a Neandertal ancestor only a few generations back.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: These people belonged to a modern human migration into Europe not previously known from the genetic record, and offer evidence of some continuity between the earliest modern humans in Europe and later Eurasians. The later Bacho Kiro individual BK1653 is more like later Europeans, such as Goyet Q116-1 and the Vestonice cluster.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only three individuals from one cave are sampled. The graph models are one set of possible fits and they put the link between Tianyuan and Goyet Q116-1 differently from the earlier study. The IUP is a technological label, and it is debated whether it marks a dispersal of people.

populations.name: Ust'-Ishim individual
populations.description: A single man who lived about 45,000 years ago in western Siberia. His genome comes from a population that lived before, or around the time of, the separation of western and eastern Eurasian populations.

membership.notes: One individual.

caveats: A single individual: a population of one is a placeholder for an otherwise unsampled group.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Ust'-Ishim is a single man known from a femur found on the banks of the Irtysh river near Ust'-Ishim in western Siberia. It was radiocarbon dated to about 45,000 years ago. His genome has been sequenced to high quality. A population of one is a placeholder for an otherwise unsampled group.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: His genetic diversity is similar to present-day Eurasians' and not Africans'. He carries as much Neandertal ancestry as present-day Eurasians, but in much longer segments, which places the Neandertal gene flow 7,000-13,000 years before he lived. He derives from a population that lived before, or around the time of, the separation of western and eastern Eurasians.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: He derives from the shared non-African population that received Neandertal gene flow. Studies find that Ust'-Ishim, like Oase 1, did not contribute detectably to later Eurasians. A deeper split, the Zlaty kun/Ranis population, separated earlier from the Out-of-Africa lineage than the one he represents. That earlier branch left no detectable descendants either.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: One man cannot show the diversity of his time and place. The Neandertal gene-flow date depends on the mutation rate used. His lineage is not shown to be directly ancestral to any present-day people. His radiocarbon date spans about 3,700 years (46,880-43,210 cal BP).

populations.name: Oase 1
populations.description: An early modern human from Peştera cu Oase, Romania, about 40,000 years ago, with a Neandertal ancestor only four to six generations back.

membership.notes: AADR labels Oase 1 as Romania_IUP.

caveats: A single individual.
AADR flags this individual's data as CRITICAL (quality/contamination warning); it is shown with that warning because it is the subject of the cited study.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Oase 1 is a single early modern human from Pestera cu Oase in Romania, about 37,000-42,000 years old. The specimen holds only small amounts of human DNA, so researchers used an enrichment method. The data flag a quality warning, shown with this entry because the paper cited here is about him.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: About 6-9% of his genome comes from Neandertals, more than any other modern human sequenced to date, with three segments longer than 50 centimorgans. That points to a Neandertal ancestor four to six generations back. A later reanalysis gives 6.4% (95% CI 5.7-7.1%).

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Oase 1 does not share more alleles with later Europeans than with East Asians, which suggests his population did not contribute substantially to later humans in Europe. Early Bacho Kiro individuals also had very recent Neandertal ancestors, so such mixing appears to have been repeated.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Neandertal share is an estimate from a very low-coverage genome with a quality warning in the data. One individual cannot show how common recent Neandertal ancestry was in his group. The 'four to six generations' figure comes from segment lengths and carries statistical uncertainty.

populations.name: Tianyuan individual
populations.description: A man who lived about 40,000 years ago near present-day Beijing, more closely related to Asians than to Europeans but with an unexpected link to a 35,000-year-old individual from Belgium.

membership.notes: One individual.

caveats: A single individual.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Tianyuan is a single man who lived about 40,000 years ago in Tianyuan Cave near Beijing in northern China. DNA enriched at 3.7 million positions gave about 3-fold average coverage. He is more closely related to Asians than to Europeans. A population of one stands in for a much larger group.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: He is more related to present-day and ancient East and Southeast Asians than to Europeans, but not a direct ancestor of any tested group. He shares extra alleles with the 35,000-year-old Goyet Q116-1 of Belgium. He carried about 4-5% Neandertal DNA, similar to other Upper Palaeolithic Eurasians.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Tianyuan belonged to a population that diverged before the ancestors of present-day East and Southeast Asians. Early European and Asian populations did not split in one clean step. The Bacho Kiro individuals relate to populations that also contributed to Tianyuan, and Tianyuan shares extra alleles with some South American groups, which fits Asian structure persisting until the Americas were settled.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: One individual with 3-fold coverage cannot show the diversity of Upper Palaeolithic East Asia. The shared affinity with Goyet Q116-1 is read differently by two studies: gene flow versus a common deep ancestry. The authors caution that their admixture model is unlikely to reflect the true history in detail.

populations.name: Early European founder population (Kostenki/Sunghir-related)
populations.description: Individuals from western Russia, about 38,000–32,000 years ago, who belong to the founder population that contributed to all later sampled European hunter-gatherers until about 14,000 years ago.

membership.notes: Kostenki 14 is the type individual in Fu 2016; Sunghir is grouped with it as related to the Věstonice cluster in Posth 2023.

caveats: Grouping Kostenki and Sunghir together is our simplification; both papers treat them as related members of the early European founder lineage.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This label groups individuals from western Russia, sampled at Kostenki and Sunghir, who lived about 38,000-32,000 years ago. They belong to an early European founder lineage, a source of ancestry for many later hunter-gatherers. The grouping is our own convenience: the studies treat Kostenki and Sunghir as related members of that lineage, not as one named population. The archaeological association of Kostenki 14 is uncertain.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Fu and colleagues (2016) find that every sampled European from Kostenki 14 (about 37,000 years ago) until about 14,000 years ago descends from this one founder population, with no evidence of major gene flow from elsewhere in that span. They find no support for an earlier claim that Kostenki 14 carried Basal Eurasian or Mal'ta-related lineages. Earlier individuals such as Oase 1 did not contribute substantially to later Europeans.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Ancestry related to Kostenki 14 and Sunghir contributed to the Vestonice-cluster Gravettian-associated people of central and southern Europe. In an admixture graph, the Vestonice cluster results from mixing between a Sunghir-related lineage and a lineage related to Goyet Q116-1. Ancient North Siberians were distantly related to these early western Eurasians.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only a handful of individuals represent a lineage spread over thousands of years and kilometres. The studies use the sampled genomes as stand-ins for unsampled populations, so the labels are shorthand. Kostenki 14's cultural association is uncertain, and the grouping of Kostenki with Sunghir is a simplification we made.

populations.name: Goyet Q116-1-related individuals (Aurignacian-associated)
populations.description: Individuals from Goyet Cave in Belgium, about 35,000 years ago, associated with the Aurignacian. Their ancestry reappears later in western European groups.

membership.notes: Goyet Q116-1 and Q376-3.

caveats: Two individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This group is two individuals from Goyet Cave in Belgium, Goyet Q116-1 and Goyet Q376-3, who lived about 35,000 years ago and are associated with the Aurignacian, a tool tradition of early modern humans in Europe. They carry similar ancestry. This pair and the later Fournol cluster both include people with mitochondrial haplogroup M, a maternal lineage not found in Europeans after the Last Glacial Maximum, the coldest phase of the last Ice Age.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Goyet Q116-1 belongs to the lineage leading to present-day Europeans, but on a different deep branch from the Vestonice cluster. It also shares extra alleles with Tianyuan, an early individual from China, so early European and Asian populations did not split cleanly in one step.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Ancestry like Goyet Q116-1 reappears 15,000 years later. At least half of the ancestry of Magdalenian-associated El Miron cluster individuals comes from the Goyet Q116-1 cluster. Fournol-cluster Gravettian-associated individuals of western Europe are a sister lineage, and Fournol-related ancestry is the better match for later Magdalenian-associated groups.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only two individuals are sampled. The two main studies disagree about how to classify the Gravettian-associated individuals at the same cave: one assigns them to the Vestonice cluster, while the later study finds them intermediate between two clusters. The sampled people may not represent everyone who lived in Europe 35,000 years ago.

populations.name: Věstonice cluster (Gravettian-associated, central and southern Europe)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers buried with Gravettian material in central and southern Europe, about 34,000–26,000 years ago, who share a genetic profile distinct from that of Gravettian-associated people further west.
populations.archaeological_context: Gravettian. The same archaeological culture is associated with two genetic profiles (see Fournol cluster).

membership.notes: Sites named by Posth 2023: Dolní Věstonice, Pavlov, Krems-Wachtberg, Paglicci, Ostuni.

caveats: The Gravettian-associated individuals from Goyet (Belgium) are assigned to this cluster by Fu 2016 but described as intermediate by Posth 2023; they are left unassigned here.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Vestonice cluster is a genetic grouping of hunter-gatherers buried with Gravettian material in central and southern Europe, with sites in Czechia, Austria and Italy. Fu and colleagues (2016) define it from genetic data first and compare it with archaeology afterwards, with 14 individuals from 34,000-26,000 years ago. These people were buried with grave goods, ornaments and ochre, in the open air or in caves.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Posth and colleagues (2023) show that Gravettian-associated people form two distinct genetic clusters, so one culture does not mean one population. The Vestonice cluster is modelled as a mix of a Sunghir-related lineage (from eastern Europe) and a lineage related to Goyet Q116-1 (from the west). It carries ancestry from the early European founder population.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Kostenki and Sunghir ancestry contributed to the Vestonice cluster. After the Last Glacial Maximum, no descendants of this ancestry were found in the same regions. In Italy, a genetic turnover brought Villabruna-cluster ancestry in place of it, which may match changes in the archaeological record.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The two main studies treat the Gravettian-associated individuals at Goyet in Belgium differently, so those individuals are left unassigned here. Sampling is thin: a few individuals at a handful of sites stand in for a cluster covering thousands of years. The authors of the earlier study interpret Venus figurines shared with Siberia as diffusion of ideas; this is one reading, not proof.

populations.name: Fournol cluster (Gravettian-associated, western Europe)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers buried with Gravettian material in France and northeastern Iberia, about 31,000–26,000 years ago. Their ancestry resembles that of earlier Aurignacian-associated individuals from Belgium.

membership.notes: Sites named by Posth 2023: Ormesson, La Rochette, Fournol, Mollet III, Reclau Viver.

caveats: Few individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Fournol cluster is a genetic grouping of hunter-gatherers buried with Gravettian material in western and southwestern Europe, with sites in France and northeastern Spain. The oldest, Ormesson 2988, is 31,000 years old. These individuals are consistently deposited in caves, sometimes with marks on bones. Until the 2023 study, the genetic profile of western Gravettian-associated people was undescribed.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Fournol ancestry is closely related to that of Aurignacian-associated Goyet Q116-1 from Belgium: in an admixture graph it is a sister lineage. All Fournol-cluster individuals share more with Goyet Q116-1 than with the Sunghir group. This is a different genetic profile from the Vestonice cluster, although both were associated with the Gravettian.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The Fournol profile derives from the earlier Goyet Q116-1 ancestry. It persisted through the Last Glacial Maximum in Solutrean-associated individuals and then in Magdalenian-associated groups of southwestern Europe. A Late Gravettian group at Goyet (27,000 years ago) shows a mixture of Fournol and Vestonice ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The cluster is based on only a few individuals, so it may not capture variation in the wider population. The cave burials are a pattern in the sampled individuals. The study treats the Goyet Gravettian group as intermediate and the earlier study assigned it differently.

populations.name: Ancient North Siberians (Yana)
populations.description: People who lived about 31,000 years ago at the Yana site in Arctic northeastern Siberia, distantly related to early western Eurasian hunter-gatherers.

membership.notes: Yana RHS individuals.

caveats: Two individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Ancient North Siberians are known from two individuals at the Yana RHS site, in Arctic northeastern Siberia, a site dated to about 31,600 years ago. They are the oldest, northernmost Pleistocene human remains found to date. The two were unrelated males, and their DNA gave a recent effective population size of up to 500.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Yana people are modelled as a mix: an early West Eurasian lineage plus roughly a quarter to a third from early East Asians, dated to about 39,000 years ago. They are distantly related to early western Eurasian hunter-gatherers such as those in Europe. The Mal'ta lineage of south-central Siberia can be modelled as a descendant of the Ancient North Siberian lineage.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The Mal'ta individual shares more alleles with Yana than with other western Eurasian hunter-gatherers, and the authors read the Mal'ta lineage as descended from Ancient North Siberians. Later, East Asian-related people gave rise to Native Americans and Ancient Paleosiberians, nearly replacing earlier inhabitants.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only two individuals from one site represent the group. There are no archaeological sites or genomes in northeastern Siberia between about 31,000 years ago and late in the Last Glacial Maximum, so the history of the lineage in that gap is unknown. The mixture proportions and dates are model estimates with wide ranges.

populations.name: Ancient North Eurasians (Mal'ta, Afontova Gora)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of south-central Siberia, about 24,000–17,000 years ago. Ancestry related to theirs later appears both in Native Americans and in western Eurasians.

membership.notes: MA-1 and Afontova Gora individuals.

caveats: Three individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Ancient North Eurasians are hunter-gatherers of south-central Siberia around the Lake Baikal region, known from the Mal'ta individual MA-1 (about 24,000 years ago) and Afontova Gora individuals (about 17,000 years ago). Few people are sampled, and the name is a genetic label for ancestry, not a named society. MA-1 is closely related to Native Americans, without close affinity to East Asians.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: MA-1 is basal to present-day western Eurasians: it branched off from the lineage leading to them early. Its mitochondrial haplogroup U also occurs in European hunter-gatherers. The Ancient North Siberian lineage found at Yana is modelled as an ancestor of the Mal'ta lineage. The 2014 study estimated that 14-38% of Native American ancestry may come from a population related to MA-1.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Ancient North Eurasian ancestry appears in western Eurasians today through later steppe movements, not through Ice Age Europeans. Most present-day Europeans can be modelled with ancestry from West European hunter-gatherers, Early European Farmers and Ancient North Eurasians. Eastern hunter-gatherers carried ancestry related to the Mal'ta individual.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Few individuals are sampled, and the Afontova Gora-2 genome has low coverage and substantial present-day contamination. The Native American share depends on the model: it is a wide range that later studies model differently. The label is a genetic abstraction built on a handful of genomes.

populations.name: Solutrean-associated individuals
populations.description: People buried with Solutrean material in Iberia and southern France during the Last Glacial Maximum, carrying ancestry related to the earlier Fournol cluster.
caveats: Very few individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Solutrean is an archaeological culture of southwestern Europe, dated about 24,000-19,000 years ago, in the coldest phase of the last Ice Age. The 2023 study reported the first genomes from Solutrean-associated people: Le Piage II in southwestern France (23,000 years ago) and La Riera, level 14, in northern Spain (21,000 years ago). Only a very small number of people are known.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Both genomes show affinity to the Fournol and GoyetQ2 clusters. Le Piage II falls close to Fournol-cluster individuals, closer to them than to the Vestonice cluster, and sits between Fournol and the later El Miron individual. So the Solutrean-associated ancestry resembles the Gravettian-associated Fournol cluster.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Fournol-related ancestry persisted through the Last Glacial Maximum in Solutrean-associated individuals and then in Magdalenian-associated people. The authors take Le Piage II as direct evidence of genetic continuity through the glacial maximum in southwestern and western Europe, which they see as a refuge for people during that time.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The conclusion of continuity rests on two genomes, one from France and one from Spain, so the picture is very thin. The studies model Solutrean-associated ancestry using stand-in genomes. Continuity is shown by the position of one individual between two clusters, not by dense sampling of the region.

populations.name: Magdalenian-associated individuals (GoyetQ2 / El Mirón cluster)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers buried with Magdalenian material, about 19,000–14,000 years ago, from Iberia to Poland. Their ancestry is modelled as mostly Fournol-related with a smaller Villabruna-related share.

membership.notes: Excludes the Late Magdalenian/Federmesser individuals at Oberkassel (WHG-like).

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Magdalenian is an archaeological culture found from Iberia to Poland after the Last Glacial Maximum. This panel groups Magdalenian-associated hunter-gatherers dated about 19,000-14,000 years ago, from the oldest, El Miron in Spain, to groups in France, Germany and Poland that form the GoyetQ2 cluster. One earlier study defines 6 such individuals in an El Miron cluster.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: These people are modelled as a mix of Fournol-related ancestry and Villabruna-related ancestry. El Miron has about 43% Villabruna-related ancestry, and the others 19-29%. Fournol is a better proxy for the older component than Goyet Q116-1. In the model, the typical mix is about three quarters Fournol-related and one quarter Villabruna-related.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Fournol-related ancestry continued from Solutrean-associated to Magdalenian-associated people. At least half of the ancestry of the El Miron cluster comes from the Goyet Q116-1 cluster. From at least 14,000 years ago, Villabruna- and Oberkassel-related ancestry spread across Europe; the study reports a turnover in which Magdalenian-associated ancestry largely disappears from sampled individuals.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The proportions come from a model using two stand-in genomes, Fournol 85 and Arene Candide 16. The geographic extent of GoyetQ2 ancestry was unclear before the 2023 study, and the authors say genomes from the preceding Badegoulian culture could help explain how it formed.

populations.name: Villabruna cluster (Epigravettian-associated)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers associated with the Epigravettian in Italy, sampled from about 17,000 years ago. Their ancestry has links to the Near East and later spread across Europe.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Villabruna cluster is a genetic grouping named after a type site, the Villabruna individual from Italy. This panel includes hunter-gatherers associated with the Epigravettian culture of the Italian peninsula and Sicily, sampled from about 17,000 years ago. All sampled individuals are genetically very similar to one another, and their differences follow geography more than time.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Villabruna-cluster people carry a component related to present-day Near Easterners, which appears in Europe from about 14,000 years ago. Genetic diversity falls from north to south in Italy, lowest in Sicily where an effective population of about 70 is estimated. Some Villabruna-cluster individuals share extra alleles with East Asians.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: In Italy, a genetic turnover brought Villabruna ancestry in place of Vestonice-cluster Gravettian-associated ancestry; no proportion is published, and it might correlate with discontinuities in the archaeological record. From at least 14,000 years ago it spread from the south across Europe, and the study reports a turnover in which Magdalenian-associated ancestry largely disappears from sampled individuals, without giving a single proportion. Magdalenian-associated groups already carry a Villabruna-related share, and Eastern hunter-gatherers also carry some.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The source of the Near Eastern-related component is unsettled. Fu and colleagues (2016) offer migration or shifting balance between European groups as two possible explanations, and the Satsurblia cluster is not a direct source. The Balkan origin proposed in 2023 is an inference from genetic distances. The Sicilian individuals reflect a very small population and may not represent the mainland.

populations.name: Western hunter-gatherers (WHG / Oberkassel cluster)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of western and central Europe from about 14,000 years ago until farming, whose ancestry spread widely after the Last Glacial Maximum and later contributed to farming populations.

membership.notes: Late Glacial and Mesolithic hunter-gatherers west of the 'great divide'. Scandinavian, Baltic and Iron Gates hunter-gatherers, who carry mixed WHG/EHG ancestry, are not included.

caveats: Iberian hunter-gatherers show their own northwest–southeast substructure (Olalde 2019).

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Western hunter-gatherers (WHG) is a name for the Oberkassel cluster, hunter-gatherers west of the Black Sea-to-Baltic boundary known as the great divide, from about 14,000 years ago until farming arrived. It is a genetic label, based on ancestry. Scandinavian, Baltic and Iron Gates hunter-gatherers, who mix WHG and EHG ancestry, are left out of this panel.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: From at least 14,000 years ago, Villabruna- and Oberkassel-related ancestry spread from the south; the study reports a turnover in which Magdalenian-associated ancestry largely disappears from sampled individuals. The Oberkassel cluster is modelled as about three quarters Villabruna-related and one quarter GoyetQ2 ancestry. Hunter-gatherers west of the great divide carried no detectable EHG ancestry until about 8,000 years ago, when it reaches about 10%.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: WHG ancestry derives from the Villabruna cluster, with a smaller GoyetQ2 share. In later farming populations it returned: Middle Neolithic farmers of Germany and Spain carry 18-34% more WHG-related ancestry than Early Neolithic ones. The last individuals with mostly hunter-gatherer ancestry date to about 5,200 years ago, at Ostorf in northern Germany.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Iberian hunter-gatherers have their own north-western and south-eastern structure, so WHG does not describe them well, and their ancestry formed through repeated local mixing. Hunter-gatherers also formed a west-to-east gradient of ancestry. The label covers 14,000 years and a wide area. The much-studied Loschbour genome has lower heterozygosity than any present-day human, reflecting a strong ancestral bottleneck.

populations.name: Eastern hunter-gatherers (EHG / Sidelkino cluster)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of the eastern European forest zone, about 11,000–7,000 years ago, with ancestry related both to western hunter-gatherers and to Ancient North Eurasians.

membership.notes: Karelia (Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov area) and Samara/Sidelkino individuals, the type groups for EHG.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Eastern hunter-gatherers (EHG), called the Sidelkino cluster in the 2023 study, lived in the forest zone of eastern Europe about 11,000-7,000 years ago. The type groups are from Karelia in northwestern Russia (the Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov site, about 8,200 years ago) and from Samara and Sidelkino on the middle Volga (about 11,000 years ago). The cluster has different uniparental markers from western groups.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: EHG ancestry is a mixture: Villabruna- or Oberkassel-related ancestry plus ancestry related to Ancient North Eurasians such as the Mal'ta individual. Admixture dating places the mixing about 15,000-13,000 years ago. The study finds EHG have high affinity to the 24,000-year-old Mal'ta individual, and the Karelia and Samara groups are indistinguishable in profile. Their Y lineages include Q, R and J.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: EHG-related ancestry first appears at about 10% in central European hunter-gatherers from about 8,000 years ago, and it is one end of the Volga cline of Eneolithic steppe people. A boundary between the Black Sea and the Baltic separated differentiated hunter-gatherers: farming changed ancestry in the west, and not substantially in the east.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Villabruna- and Oberkassel-related share in early groups varied, so the cluster formed unevenly. Radiocarbon dates on the upper Volga may be up to 500 years too old because of fish in the diet. The label groups people over several thousand years and is not a single society.

populations.name: Caucasus hunter-gatherers (CHG)
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of western Georgia, about 13,300 and 9,700 years ago, who form a distinct ancient lineage. CHG-related ancestry later contributed to steppe populations.

membership.notes: Satsurblia and Kotias Klde. Older Georgian UP individuals (Dzudzuana, Kotias Klde UP) are not assigned.

caveats: Three individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Caucasus hunter-gatherers (CHG) are known from western Georgia: Satsurblia cave (about 13,300 years ago) and Kotias Klde rockshelter (about 9,700 years ago). Genome sequencing of two men there showed they form a distinct ancient lineage with continuity between the Late Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic. The group is very small and the name is a genetic label.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In model-based estimates, CHG split from western hunter-gatherers about 45,000 years ago (40-50,000 depending on the genomes used) and from the ancestors of Neolithic farmers about 25,000 years ago. CHG and early farmers form a clade relative to western hunter-gatherers. They show signs of a small population, and present-day southern Caucasus people are the closest to them in the sample.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: CHG-related ancestry contributed significantly to Yamnaya-associated steppe herders, and the Caucasus-Lower Volga cline of Eneolithic steppe people is rich in CHG-related ancestry. Caucasus hunter-gatherers (the Satsurblia cluster) are related to a population that contributed Near Eastern-related alleles to European hunter-gatherers after 14,000 years ago, but are not the direct source.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Split times are model-based and depend on which genomes and which mutation rate are used. Two or three individuals represent thousands of years in one region. The relationship to later populations is partly inferred from present-day genomes. Older Georgian Upper Palaeolithic individuals are not assigned to this group.

populations.name: Iberomaurusian-associated individuals (Taforalt)
populations.description: People buried at Taforalt cave in Morocco about 15,000 years ago, with Iberomaurusian material. Their ancestry links North Africa with the Near East and sub-Saharan Africa.
caveats: Claims verified against the abstract only.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are people buried at Taforalt cave in Morocco about 15,000 years ago with Iberomaurusian material, an archaeological culture. The study sequenced seven individuals dated to about 15,000 years ago. The label is archaeological, so it does not by itself define a population. Taforalt is in Morocco, in northwest Africa.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Taforalt individuals show genetic affinity with early Holocene Near Easterners, best represented by Natufians, and no evidence of gene flow from Palaeolithic Europeans. About one third of their ancestry is related to sub-Saharan Africans. That part is best approximated by a mix of components found in present-day West and East Africans.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: This overview rests on the abstract of the paper only, because the full text is not openly available, so the details of the models and the sampling are not checked. The sub-Saharan part is described with present-day proxies, which may not match any ancient group. Seven individuals from one cave may not represent all of North Africa at the time.

populations.name: Natufian-associated hunter-gatherers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of the southern Levant associated with the Natufian culture, before the beginning of farming. About half their ancestry is modelled as coming from a 'Basal Eurasian' lineage.
caveats: Few individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Natufian-associated people were hunter-gatherers of the southern Levant who lived before farming began. The main ancient-DNA study sampled them from Raqefet Cave, dated about 12,000-9,800 BCE. The label comes from an archaeological culture, and only a few individuals are sampled. Natufians and later Levantine farmers carried Y chromosome haplogroup E.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: About 44% (plus or minus 8) of Natufian ancestry is modelled as coming from a Basal Eurasian lineage, an early branch of non-African people that is known only through its traces in other groups. A later study, using a different reference, estimates 38.5% (plus or minus 5). The study found no genome-wide affinity between Natufians and sub-Saharan Africans.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The first farmers of the southern Levant descended largely from local Natufian-related hunter-gatherers: they share more alleles with Natufians than with early farmers of Iran. The people of Taforalt in Morocco also show genetic affinity with Natufians, a finding read from the study's abstract only.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Basal Eurasian share depends on the method and reference used, and it has no sampled individuals of its own. The Natufian sample is from a single cave. The authors suggest that further Natufians from other sites, and ancient DNA from North Africa, could improve understanding of their origin.

populations.name: Anatolian Epipalaeolithic hunter-gatherer (Pınarbaşı)
populations.description: A hunter-gatherer from Pınarbaşı in central Anatolia, about 15,000 years ago, whose ancestry continues to a large degree in the region's first farmers.
caveats: A single individual.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This group is one person, a hunter-gatherer from Pinarbasi in central Anatolia directly dated to 13,642-13,073 cal BCE, about 15,000 years ago. This is the first Epipaleolithic Anatolian genome sequenced. It sits between western European hunter-gatherers and Levantine populations in a PCA, and is distinct from both.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Pinarbasi genome has about 25% Basal Eurasian ancestry in one estimate, a modelled early lineage of non-Africans. He shares extra alleles with both western hunter-gatherers and Levantine Natufians, but is distinct from each. The Basal Eurasian estimate depends on the method and reference used.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Central Anatolian early farmers show about 80-90% genetic continuity with this hunter-gatherer. Aceramic farmers derive about 90% from AHG-related ancestry, with the rest Iranian/Caucasus-related; later farmers add Levant Neolithic-related ancestry. The authors read this as a limited role of migration in the emergence of farming in central Anatolia, and see a link with Iron Gates hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: A single individual stands for central Anatolia 15,000 years ago, so personal variation cannot be separated from group variation. The farmers' continuity figure is a model estimate with uncertainty. The link to Balkan hunter-gatherers is an inference from allele sharing and the authors treat it as a possibility. The result concerns central Anatolia and does not apply to all of Anatolia.

populations.name: Basal Eurasian lineage (modelled)
populations.description: A modelled ancestral lineage that split from other non-African lineages before they diversified. It is needed to fit the ancestry of early Near Easterners and Early European Farmers, but no individual from it has been sampled.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: The time range is a display window only: the papers place the lineage's split before the diversification of other non-Africans and its contribution before the earliest sampled Natufians, without dating it precisely.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Basal Eurasian is not a sampled group but a modelled lineage. Researchers propose it to fit the data: a lineage that split from other non-African people before they diversified. It is needed to explain the ancestry of early Near Easterners and the first European farmers. No individual from it has been sequenced. The dates on the timeline are a display window, not an estimate.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Estimates of its contribution come from statistical models. Early European Farmers are modelled with about 44% (plus or minus 10). The highest Near Eastern estimates are 66% in a Mesolithic Iranian, 48% in Iranian Neolithic and 44% in Natufians. A later study using another reference finds lower values for Natufians (38.5%). The lineage is inferred to have had little or no Neanderthal ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The lineage has no sampled members, so where and when it lived is unknown, and the authors offer two different scenarios. Its Neanderthal share is a wide range (0-60%). Estimates vary with method and reference. Earlier claims of Basal Eurasian ancestry in European Ice Age individuals were not supported by a later study.

populations.name: Early farmers of the Zagros
populations.description: Early Neolithic people of the Zagros mountains in western Iran, among the earliest farmers, who descended largely from local hunter-gatherers and were genetically distinct from Anatolian and Levantine farmers.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are Early Neolithic people of the Zagros mountains in western Iran, among the earliest farmers. The studies sequenced a handful of individuals: Wezmeh Cave (about 7,455-7,082 BCE) and Tepe Abdul Hosein (about 10,000 years old), plus Ganj Dareh farmers dated 8,200-7,600 BCE. Isotopes in one individual indicate a diet rich in cultivated cereals.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The first farmers of the Zagros descended largely from local hunter-gatherers and were strongly different from those of the Levant. They carry about 48% Basal Eurasian ancestry in one model. They share alleles equally with Anatolian and Levantine farmers, suggesting long isolation. Their ancestors are modelled as separating from Anatolian farmers' ancestors 46,000-77,000 years ago.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Zagros people were neither ancestral to the first European farmers nor important to present-day Europeans. Later Iranian Chalcolithic populations, related to them, spread widely: one is modelled as contributing about 43% of Early Bronze Age steppe ancestry and about 44% of Levantine Bronze Age ancestry. Whether Iranian farmers spread to South Asia is contested.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The 46,000-77,000 year split is a model estimate with a wide interval. Only a few individuals are sampled, with low coverage for most. Later Iranian Chalcolithic ancestry derives from several sources, so contributions cannot be tied to farmers alone. Some conclusions rest on comparisons with present-day genomes.

populations.name: Early farmers of the southern Levant (PPNB)
populations.description: Pre-Pottery Neolithic farmers of Jordan and Israel, who descended largely from local Natufian-related hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are Pre-Pottery Neolithic farmers of Jordan and Israel, buried at sites such as 'Ain Ghazal, Motza, Kfar HaHoresh and Ba'ja between about 8,300 and 6,700 BCE. They are among the first farmers of the southern Levant. The studies sample very few individuals from a small number of sites.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The first farmers of the southern Levant descended largely from local Natufian-related hunter-gatherers: about two thirds of their ancestry is Natufian-related, and about one third is related to Anatolian farmers, in one model. They were strongly different from the first farmers of the Zagros.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Natufian-related hunter-gatherers are the main source. Later, Levant, Zagros and Anatolia-related farmer ancestries mixed by the Bronze Age, and Late Chalcolithic Peqi'in Cave people are modelled as about 57% Levant Neolithic-related. Levant-related ancestry may also have reached East Africa, as pastoralists there carry about 38% Levantine-related ancestry in one model.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Whether the Levant-related ancestry in East Africa came by migration or from a shared earlier ancestral population is open. The proportions are model estimates. A few individuals from a few sites stand for the whole region over about 1,600 years, and the Levant-related ancestry in East Africa is dated and modelled using proxy groups.

populations.name: Early farmers of Anatolia
populations.description: Neolithic farmers of central and western Anatolia, whose ancestry continues largely from local hunter-gatherers and is closely related to that of the first farmers of Europe.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are Neolithic farmers of central and western Anatolia. In the central region, the study sampled aceramic farmers at Boncuklu (about 8300-7800 BCE) and later ceramic-period farmers; northwestern Anatolian Neolithic farmers form the reference for the first European farmers. The people are grouped by the archaeological stage they belong to.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Central Anatolian early farmers show about 80-90% genetic continuity with a local 15,000-year-old hunter-gatherer from Pinarbasi, plus Iranian/Caucasus-related ancestry earlier and Levant-related ancestry later. Their ancestors are modelled as separating from the Zagros farmers' ancestors tens of thousands of years earlier.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Farmer ancestry related to Anatolian farmers spread west into Europe. Farming reached southeastern Europe in the mid-7th millennium BCE with migrants of Anatolian-related ancestry, and Balkan Neolithic populations derive about 98% of their ancestry from Anatolian-related sources in one model. Early farmers of Iberia and Britain also carry mostly Anatolian-farmer-related ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Sampling is concentrated in a few sites in central and northwestern Anatolia, and the spatial distribution of Anatolian-like farmers is unknown, so the source of the European farmers is not pinned down. The continuity figure for central Anatolia is a model estimate. Split dates are model-based with wide intervals.

populations.name: Late Chalcolithic individuals of Peqi'in Cave
populations.description: People buried in Peqi'in Cave, northern Israel, during the Late Chalcolithic (about 4500–3900 BCE). They formed a homogeneous population modelled with Levantine, Iranian-related and Anatolian-related ancestry.
populations.archaeological_context: Late Chalcolithic of the southern Levant.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are people buried in Peqi'in Cave in northern Israel during the Late Chalcolithic (Copper Age) period, about 4500-3900 BCE. The 2018 study analysed 22 individuals from the cave, of whom 20 appear unrelated, and found them to be a genetically homogeneous population. Nine of the ten males carry the same Y chromosome lineage, haplogroup T.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The Peqi'in population is modelled as about 57% Levant Neolithic-related, 17% Iran Chalcolithic-related and 26% Anatolian Neolithic-related. By the Bronze Age, Levant-, Zagros- and Anatolia-related farmer ancestries had mixed and differences across the Near East had shrunk. Peqi'in people were therefore already a mix of sources at about 4500 BCE.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Peqi'in people descend in part from the local Levant Neolithic, but were formed partly by outside influences from Iranian and Anatolian sources. Earlier Levantine populations were dominated by a different Y lineage. The Peqi'in population contributed differently to later Bronze Age groups, and one of those could not plausibly have descended from the same population.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Several similar three-way models fit, so the sources are proxies and not exact ancestors. One cave sample may not represent the whole southern Levant, and the percentages are model estimates, not counts of ancestors. The result describes this cave population only, and the claim that movements of people drove cultural change is the authors' inference.

populations.name: Early farmers associated with Starčevo–Körös–Criș
populations.description: The first farming communities of southeastern Europe from the mid-7th millennium BCE, carrying ancestry mostly related to Anatolian farmers.
populations.archaeological_context: Starčevo, Körös and Criș complexes; Early Neolithic of Greece.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are the first farming communities of southeastern Europe, associated with the Starcevo-Koros-Cris archaeological cultures, from the mid-7th millennium BCE. Farming reached the region with migrants of Anatolian-related ancestry. The label groups people by archaeological context, and it covers communities that differed from each other in how much local hunter-gatherer ancestry they carried.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Balkan Neolithic populations derive about 98% (95% CI 97-100%) of their ancestry from northwestern Anatolian-related farmers. Exceptions show local mixing: eight of nine Malak Preslavets individuals are modelled with about 15% western hunter-gatherer and 4% eastern hunter-gatherer ancestry. Most early Neolithic Hungarians do not differ significantly from Neolithic Anatolians.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The first farmers of northern and western Europe passed through southeastern Europe with limited hunter-gatherer admixture, and the first farmers of central Europe descended from groups that did. Some groups that remained mixed extensively. Hunter-gatherer ancestry rose again in the Balkans in the Copper Age.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Groups such as Malak Preslavets, Lepenski Vir and the southern Greek sites differ from each other, so one average does not describe the region. The southern Greek individuals show Caucasus-related shifts whose source is uncertain. Dating and sampling vary between sites.

populations.name: LBK-associated farmers
populations.description: Farmers of the Linear Pottery (LBK) culture across central Europe, about 5500–4900 BCE, with mostly Anatolian-farmer-related ancestry and a small hunter-gatherer share.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are farmers buried with Linear Pottery (LBK) material across central Europe, about 5500-4900 BCE. The Lipson study pooled LBK samples from Stuttgart with others farther northeast, such as Halberstadt. Early farmers in Germany, Hungary and Spain were closely related to each other and distinct from local hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: LBK ancestry is mostly early European farmer-related, from Anatolian-related ancestry, with about 4-5% hunter-gatherer ancestry. Admixture is dated to about 5545 BCE (plus or minus 65). The early farmers are also modelled with Basal Eurasian ancestry, about 44% (plus or minus 10), in one model that fits the ancestry of Stuttgart.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The first farmers of central Europe descended from groups that passed through southeastern Europe with limited hunter-gatherer admixture. Later, hunter-gatherer ancestry returned: German Middle Neolithic groups have about 17%, and 18-34% more western hunter-gatherer ancestry than the Early Neolithic in Germany and Spain.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Hunter-gatherer source populations for LBK mixing are not statistically settled. The LBK sample pools several sites and phases. Hunter-gatherer ancestry varied by site, with some farmers far above the average. Sex bias in later admixture is inferred from the X chromosome.

populations.name: Early Neolithic farmers of Iberia
populations.description: Early farmers of the Iberian Peninsula, including Cardial-associated individuals, from the mid-6th millennium BCE.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are early farmers of the Iberian peninsula, including people associated with the Cardial culture, from the mid-6th millennium BCE. The 2017 and 2019 studies sampled them. Farming is thought to have begun in Spain around 5500 BCE. Local hunter-gatherers there showed strong differences between the northwest and southeast before farming.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Early farmers of Iberia carried mostly Anatolian-farmer-related ancestry, with some hunter-gatherer ancestry from local admixture. Admixture is dated about 5650 BCE on average, and some hunter-gatherer ancestry may have been acquired on the way. Hunter-gatherer ancestry increased: about 23% in the Iberian Middle Neolithic and about 27% in the Chalcolithic.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Most Copper Age Iberians resemble earlier Iberian populations. Iberian Neolithic genomes also resemble British and Irish ones, suggesting a Mediterranean route for farmers who reached Britain. Middle Neolithic populations of Germany and Spain carry about 18-34% more western hunter-gatherer ancestry than Early Neolithic ones.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The earliest Iberian farmers are few, and admixture dates are estimates with uncertainty. The hunter-gatherer source in early farmers is not identified in detail, since only one hunter-gatherer-related component could be confidently detected. The Mediterranean route to Britain is an inference from genetic similarity.

populations.name: Neolithic farmers of Britain
populations.description: Farming communities of Britain from about 4000 BCE, whose ancestry derives mainly from continental farmers, with small, regionally varying contributions from local hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are farmers buried in Britain from about 4000 BCE onward, from the earliest Neolithic (about 3951-3780 BCE in Scotland) to the Late Neolithic (about 2570-2347 BCE in Orkney). The 2019 study analysed 67 of them, together with six earlier hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: British Neolithic individuals carry mostly Anatolian-farmer-related ancestry: over 56% in every individual and about 74% on average in the study's model, with the rest from hunter-gatherers. Hunter-gatherer ancestry varies by region: lowest in Wales, higher in south-east England and Scotland. The authors found no later hunter-gatherer resurgence.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The farmers arrived by 3975-3722 cal BCE and resemble Iberian and Irish Neolithic farmers, consistent with a Mediterranean route. British Mesolithic people cluster with western hunter-gatherers and are not the main ancestors of Neolithic Britons. Later, Beaker-associated people carried high steppe-related ancestry and the study estimates about 90% of Britain's gene pool was replaced within a few centuries.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The proportions are model estimates and vary between individuals. Only six Mesolithic genomes represent local hunter-gatherers. Where the farmers' ancestors lived on the continent is inferred from similarity to Iberian and Irish genomes, not shown directly. Small numbers per region limit comparisons of regional differences.

populations.name: Trypillia-associated farmers
populations.description: Farmers of the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture in present-day Ukraine and Moldova during the Eneolithic.

region.name: Forest-steppe north of the Black Sea

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Cucuteni-Trypillia (Trypillia for short) was a farming culture of the Eneolithic, the Copper Age, in what is now Ukraine and Moldova. This panel groups sampled individuals by that archaeological label, so it describes people attributed to a culture, not a single genetic population. The 2025 North Pontic study describes the culture as spreading east across the Carpathian mountains to the Dnipro Valley around 4800 BCE, and its ancestry as mainly derived from early European farmers.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In the 2025 study, 23 of 24 sampled Trypillia individuals fit a three-source model. On average it gives about 81% Balkan Eneolithic farmer-related ancestry, 14% Balkan hunter-gatherer-related ancestry and 5% ancestry from the Caucasus-Lower Volga (CLV) cline. The CLV cline is a gradient of ancestry between the Caucasus and the lower Volga. The authors date the formative mixing to about 4595 BCE (95% interval 4832-4358 BCE).

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Trypillia farmers contributed ancestry to the Usatove-associated people. Usatove is modelled as about 55% Trypillia-associated farmers and about 45% a CLV-cline group, with mixing dated to about 4471 BCE. The authors suggest several settings for the contact, among them an outpost, a coexisting 'commonwealth' of cultures, or dominance by CLV-related groups, and say the genetic data do not decide between them.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: One of the 24 sampled individuals did not fit the model. The percentages are statistical estimates that rest on stand-in source groups, not on directly sampled ancestors, so they carry uncertainty beyond any single figure. The proportion of hunter-gatherer ancestry in Trypillia is known only at this coarse level, and the authors give no finer account of where it came from.

populations.name: Globular Amphora-associated individuals
populations.description: Late Neolithic people of central and eastern Europe associated with the Globular Amphora culture, about 3400–2800 BCE.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Globular Amphora is an archaeological culture of the Late Neolithic in central and eastern Europe, and this panel groups sampled people buried in that context in Poland and Czechia. The Bohemian archaeology study places it in the Middle Eneolithic, about 3500-2800 BCE, alongside the Baden and Rivnac cultures. Culture labels can hide mixed communities, so the group may include people of varied ancestry.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In Bohemia, Globular Amphora individuals carry the largest share of hunter-gatherer-related ancestry among the groups just before Corded Ware, about 26% on average in one model. The date of that hunter-gatherer mixing is not later than in the neighbouring Rivnac group. This suggests the Bohemian burials reflect people arriving from elsewhere, perhaps Poland. They show no detectable steppe ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Allentoft and colleagues (2024) find that the farmer-related ancestry in Corded Ware-associated individuals can be modelled as coming only from a Globular Amphora-associated cluster. They infer that steppe-related ancestry spread largely through groups that had already mixed with Globular Amphora-related farmers. They place the contact zone with Yamnaya-related groups northwest of the Black Sea. Other studies model farmer ancestry in some Yamnaya groups using Globular Amphora as a stand-in, with about 13-17%, and two Moldovan outliers fit with it as a source.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The two lines of evidence are not fully aligned. The Bohemian burials show no steppe ancestry, while the wider modelling links this farmer-related ancestry with steppe ancestry elsewhere. Sampling is uneven, since most individuals come from a few regions. The connections rest on statistical proxies, and earlier work using few genomes had suggested contact in this zone was only cultural.

populations.name: Volga cline Eneolithic (Khvalynsk, Ekaterinovka)
populations.description: Eneolithic people of the middle Volga whose ancestry varies between Caucasus–Lower Volga-related and eastern hunter-gatherer-related ends of a cline.
caveats: Individuals on a cline are genetically heterogeneous by definition.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This group holds Eneolithic (Copper Age) people from sites along the middle Volga river, such as Khvalynsk and Ekaterinovka, who share one pattern. Their ancestry falls along a gradient, called a cline: from Eastern hunter-gatherer ancestry upriver to ancestry from the Lower Volga at the other end. Because it is a gradient, members differ a lot from one another; the authors describe some groups as hyper-variable.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: Ekaterinovka burials are dated 5050-4450 BCE and Khvalynsk 4500-4350 BCE, from herbivore-bone radiocarbon dates. One person with a Volga-cline profile was buried far away at Csongrad in Hungary (4331-4073 BCE), which the authors read as long-distance contact. Sampling clusters on a few sites along one river, so the cline reflects those places and not the whole region.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The study models these people as a mix of Lower Volga (Berezhnovka-related) ancestry and Eastern hunter-gatherer ancestry. At Ekaterinovka about 24% is Berezhnovka-related. At Khvalynsk the share ranges from about 41% to 77% between individuals, and across the whole cline from roughly 14% to 89%. The gradient is the evidence that upriver and downriver communities mixed.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The upriver, Eastern hunter-gatherer end of the cline has long-established antecedents in eastern Europe, while the Lower Volga end does not. The same study finds that the later Yamnaya cannot be traced to the Volga cline: their profile places them on a separate cline along the Dnipro river. The Volga cline is therefore a neighbour and relative of Yamnaya ancestors, not a direct ancestor.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Where Lower Volga ancestry came from is unknown. No earlier genomes have been sequenced from that area, and a Caucasus hunter-gatherer-related source has not been sampled. The percentages are model estimates using stand-in source groups. Individuals on a cline differ by definition, so group averages hide real variation.

populations.name: Caucasus–Lower Volga cline Eneolithic (Berezhnovka)
populations.description: Eneolithic people of the lower Volga steppe at the northern end of a genetic cline rich in Caucasus hunter-gatherer-related ancestry. CLV-related ancestry later makes up most of Yamnaya ancestry.

membership.notes: Only the Berezhnovka individuals are clearly labelled in AADR v66.p1; other CLV-cline sites named by Lazaridis 2025 are not assigned yet.

caveats: Membership is incomplete: assigning the remaining CLV-cline individuals needs the paper's individual list.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This group holds Eneolithic people of the Lower Volga steppe, mainly burials at Berezhnovka. They sit at the northern end of the Caucasus-Lower Volga (CLV) cline, a gradient of ancestry running from the Neolithic Caucasus to the Lower Volga. Mostly it is people whose ancestry is rich in Caucasus hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, and the label includes only some of the sites the study assigns to the cline.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: Berezhnovka-2 burials date to about 4450-3960 BCE on the Lower Volga. The cline, as defined by the study, spans sites from Armenia to the Lower Volga, including Maikop, Progress-2 and Remontnoye in the North Caucasus and nearby steppe. Only a few sites are sampled, and no earlier individuals are known from the Lower Volga itself.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The cline is modelled as mixing between Neolithic Caucasus ancestry (Aknashen-related) and Lower Volga ancestry. The main Maikop cluster is about 86% Aknashen-related, while Remontnoye has roughly 45%. Berezhnovka-2 itself also carries about 29% Central Asian, Siberian-related ancestry in one model, which another Lower Don group lacks. These figures are modelled shares from stand-in source groups.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: CLV-related people are modelled as contributing about four-fifths of Yamnaya ancestry, and about half of Usatove-associated ancestry, but only about 5% of Trypillia. CLV ancestry also appears in Chalcolithic Armenia at Areni-1, and at least a tenth of Bronze Age central Anatolian ancestry. The authors cannot fix the exact steppe-related source in Anatolia.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The roster is incomplete, because only Berezhnovka burials are labelled here and other CLV sites are not yet assigned. The origin of Lower Volga ancestry is unknown. The sources that formed Yamnaya may have differed from the sampled Remontnoye and Serednii Stih individuals, which the authors say stand in for unsampled groups.

populations.name: Serednii Stih-associated individuals (Dnipro cline)
populations.description: Eneolithic people of the Dnipro and Don steppe associated with the Serednii Stih culture, formed as Caucasus–Lower Volga-related people mixed with Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherers. Yamnaya ancestors formed from related groups.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Serednii Stih is an archaeological complex of the Eneolithic (Copper Age) in the Dnipro and Don steppe. The 2025 study samples it with 13 individuals, and their ancestry varies widely between people. That variety is the main finding: they sit along a gradient called the Dnipro cline, from hunter-gatherer-rich ancestry to ancestry similar to Yamnaya.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Serednii Stih people are modelled as migrants with ancestry from the Caucasus-Lower Volga (CLV) cline who mixed with local Dnipro-Don hunter-gatherers. Each Stih group fits a mix of hunter-gatherer ancestry and Core Yamnaya-like ancestry, in varying proportions. The study finds no appreciable European-farmer ancestry in them. For comparison, Yamnaya are inferred to have about a fifth of their ancestry from the hunter-gatherer source.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Yamnaya ancestors are modelled as forming around 4000 BCE from Serednii Stih-related groups. A Yamnaya-like individual from Mykhailivka (3635-3383 BCE) bridges the sampled Stih and Yamnaya individuals. The authors treat Core Yamna as a late Stih-derived population with more CLV-related ancestry than the sampled Stih individuals.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only 13 individuals represent a culture that is dated across more than a thousand years, so the sample is thin. Radiocarbon dates are uncorrected for freshwater fish in the diet and may be too old. The study uses Core Yamnaya as a stand-in for an unsampled earlier population, which the authors call ahistorical. Whether the local hunter-gatherer source is best shown by Dnipro or Middle Don people is also unclear.

populations.name: Maikop-associated individuals (North Caucasus)
populations.description: People of the North Caucasus associated with the Maikop culture in the 4th millennium BCE, genetically closer to populations south of the Caucasus than to their steppe neighbours.

membership.notes: Steppe Maikop individuals (with additional Siberian-related ancestry, Wang 2019) are not included.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Maikop is an archaeological culture of the North Caucasus, known for rich burial mounds, and this panel groups people buried in the northern foothills. The 12 sampled individuals from eight sites look genetically uniform and resemble earlier Eneolithic people of the region. Maikop-associated people buried on the open steppe are a different group and are kept out of this panel, because their ancestry differs.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: One study models Caucasus groups, including Maikop, as a mix of Anatolian farmer-related and Caucasus hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, with ranges of 40-72% and 28-60% depending on the stand-in used. A later study models the main Maikop cluster as about 86% ancestry related to Neolithic Armenia (Aknashen). The two studies use different stand-ins, so their figures are not directly comparable.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Maikop-like ancestry continues locally for centuries in the Caucasus, until about 1100 BCE in later groups such as those of Kura-Araxes and the Late Bronze Age. The 2025 study places Maikop on the Caucasus-Lower Volga cline, an ancestry gradient linking the Caucasus to the steppe, and finds about one seventh Lower Volga ancestry in sampled Maikop. Maikop-associated burials on the open steppe differ, with extra Siberian-related ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Proportions depend on the stand-in sources. Authors of the earlier study say unsampled populations from eastern Anatolia, the South Caucasus or northern Mesopotamia could also fit, so the numbers are provisional. Dating and sampling are limited to a few sites.

populations.name: Yamnaya-associated individuals
populations.description: Herders buried in kurgans of the Yamnaya complex from about 3300 BCE, from Hungary to Kazakhstan. Genetically they are remarkably homogeneous, and ancestry related to theirs later spread widely across Europe and into Central Asia.
populations.genetic_profile: Combines Caucasus/Near Eastern-related and eastern European hunter-gatherer-related ancestry; competing models of how it formed are shown side by side.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Yamnaya is an archaeological complex of herders buried under mounds called kurgans. It appeared around 3300 BCE north of the Black and Caspian Seas and reached from Hungary to Kazakhstan by 3000 BCE. Sampled individuals are genetically very similar across that range. Relatedness analysis shows that most people buried in the same kurgan were not close relatives. The panel covers kurgan burials, which may not represent everyone who lived then.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: The Yamnaya complex appeared around 3300 BCE and reached from Hungary to Kazakhstan by 3000 BCE. In south-eastern Europe some Yamnaya-associated people cluster with the core group, while others show mixing with local Neolithic and Chalcolithic groups in the late 4th millennium BCE. The Don Yamnaya, about 79% core Yamnaya and 21% Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherer ancestry, expanded little. Almost all Core Yamnaya males carry Y lineage R-M269, while Don Yamnaya males mostly carry I-L699.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Studies agree that Yamnaya ancestry combined eastern hunter-gatherer-related and Caucasus-related ancestry, but they differ on the exact sources, so the models appear side by side. The 2025 study finds about four-fifths from the Caucasus-Lower Volga cline and the rest from Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherers, with the mixing dated near 4000 BCE. Another study models steppe ancestry as 65% Middle Don hunter-gatherer-related and 35% Caucasus hunter-gatherer-related.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Serednii Stih-related groups are modelled as the immediate ancestors, around 4000 BCE. After about 3300 BCE, Yamnaya-related ancestry spread across western Eurasia, reaching most of Europe within about a thousand years and western Mongolia after about 3000 BCE. Corded Ware-associated individuals in Germany trace about 75% of their ancestry to a Yamnaya-related source. Catacomb-complex individuals in the North Pontic region still carry Core Yamna ancestry. Bronze Age Anatolia shows negligible Yamnaya-related ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Where Yamnaya ancestry first formed is open: the Dnipro basin fits best, but the Don area cannot be excluded. The sampled Yamnaya genomes may not be the most direct source of steppe ancestry in Corded Ware groups. Core Yamnaya also stands in as a model for earlier unsampled groups. The different hunter-gatherer sources used by the models have not been reconciled.

populations.name: Corded Ware-associated individuals
populations.description: People buried with Corded Ware material across northern and central Europe from about 2900 BCE, most of whose ancestry is related to Yamnaya-associated groups.

overview.heading: Who they were
