overview.text: Corded Ware is an archaeological culture, named for pottery decorated with cord impressions, found across northern and central Europe from about 2900 BCE. This panel groups sampled people buried with that material. In Bohemia, the earliest Corded Ware burials date to about 3010-2889 BCE, and the early Corded Ware individuals there were genetically very diverse.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Corded Ware-associated individuals from Germany trace about 75% of their ancestry to a Yamnaya-related source. Modelled against Middle Neolithic farmers instead, the turnover is 48-80%. A later study models the farmer-related part as coming from a Globular Amphora-associated cluster. In Bohemia, a small extra component related to north-eastern European hunter-gatherers, about 5-15%, improves the fit.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Yamnaya-related and Globular Amphora-associated ancestry both contributed to Corded Ware-associated groups, according to Allentoft and colleagues (2024). In Bohemia, steppe ancestry first appears with Corded Ware, and none was detected in contemporary Globular Amphora and Rivnac groups. Later Bell Beaker- and Unetice-associated groups carry less steppe-related ancestry than Corded Ware, though it persisted in all sampled central Europeans.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The direct source of Corded Ware's steppe ancestry is not identified: sampled Yamnaya individuals fit only imperfectly, and Y-chromosome lineages differ between the two groups. The Bohemian authors read the early groups as plural, mixed communities, an interpretation that DNA alone does not test. The 75% figure comes from German samples and one choice of model.

populations.name: Beaker-associated individuals, central and northwest Europe
populations.description: People buried with Bell Beaker material in central and northwest Europe (outside Britain and Iberia), about 2500–2000 BCE, most of whom carry substantial steppe-related ancestry.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Bell Beaker is an archaeological complex defined by bell-shaped pots and other grave goods, found across western and central Europe. This panel groups sampled people buried with it in central and northwest Europe, outside Britain and Iberia. The 2018 study included 133 central European individuals. Beaker is a cultural label, so it does not by itself show who the people were genetically.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Most Beaker-associated individuals outside Iberia carry steppe-related ancestry. They also carry earlier farmer-related ancestry, closest to central and northern European Neolithic groups. Most males carry Y haplogroup R1b-M269 (84 of 90). In Bohemia, late Beaker individuals carry about 20% more local Middle Eneolithic-like ancestry than the three early ones.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Beaker-associated people in central Europe share steppe-related ancestry with Corded Ware-associated people, though Bell Beaker- and Unetice-associated groups carry less than Corded Ware. After Beaker, the early Bronze Age Unetice period in Bohemia shows another ancestry shift, which one model puts at 47.7% replacement and another at 63.5% early Beaker-related ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Beaker complex spread between Iberia and central Europe mainly by cultural transmission, since the two regions' Beaker-associated people had limited genetic affinity. The earliest Bohemian Beaker sample is only three people, so source populations cannot be resolved there. Paternal lineages do not link Beaker directly to Corded Ware or Yamnaya males.

populations.name: Beaker-associated individuals, Britain
populations.description: People buried with Bell Beaker material in Britain from about 2450 BCE, with high steppe-related ancestry, unlike Britain's Neolithic population.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are people in Britain buried with Bell Beaker material from about 2450 BCE. The 2018 study analysed 37 of them. They closely resemble Beaker-associated people from central Europe, and individuals from the Dutch site of Oostwoud are most closely related to those in southern Britain. Oostwoud people are close relatives of the group that moved, not necessarily its ancestors.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: British Beaker-associated individuals carry high levels of steppe-related ancestry, which is absent in the 51 Neolithic individuals from Britain studied. The authors estimate that about 90% of Britain's gene pool was replaced within a few centuries. During the first centuries, about 2450-2000 BCE, proportions varied widely, consistent with migrants who were just beginning to mix with earlier people.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Before the Beaker complex, Britain's Neolithic farmers had about 80% early European farmer and 20% western hunter-gatherer ancestry. Later, between 1000 and 875 BCE, early European farmer-related ancestry increased again in southern Britain, through migrants most similar to ancient individuals from France.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The 90% figure is a model estimate that uses the Oostwoud individuals as stand-ins for the incoming population, and the actual continental source may remain unsampled. Proportions varied between individuals in the first centuries, so one number cannot describe every community.

populations.name: Chalcolithic people of Iberia (including Beaker-associated individuals)
populations.description: Individuals from Copper Age Iberia (about 3000–2200 BCE), among them many buried with Bell Beaker material. Most resemble earlier Iberian populations and lack steppe-related ancestry, so the same pottery style travelled with different people in different places.
populations.archaeological_context: Iberian Chalcolithic, including Bell Beaker contexts.

membership.notes: AADR v66.p1 labels Iberian Beaker-associated individuals by period (e.g. Spain_C), not by culture, so Beaker association cannot be read from the label. Individuals labelled -oSteppe form a separate population.

caveats: Grouped by region and period because the AADR labels do not record Beaker association.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This panel groups people from Copper Age Iberia, about 3000-2200 BCE, by region and period. Many were buried with Bell Beaker material, but the data labels do not record that, so the panel includes people with and without it. Beaker material in Iberia did not travel with a single population: Iberian and central European Beaker-associated people had limited genetic affinity.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Among the 32 analysed Iberian Beaker-associated individuals, only 8 carry steppe-related ancestry. The Neolithic-related ancestry of Iberian Beaker individuals fits local Middle Neolithic and Copper Age groups best, not central or northern European ones. Earlier work gives the hunter-gatherer share of Iberian Chalcolithic ancestry as about 27%.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Most Copper Age Iberians resemble earlier Iberian populations, and hunter-gatherer ancestry in early European farmers generally rose through local admixture. The pattern changes after about 2500 BCE, when steppe-related ancestry appears in the Bronze Age and, by about 2000 BCE, makes up about 40% of Iberian ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Because the panel groups by region and period, it mixes people with and without Beaker material, and cannot show who chose that pottery. One Copper Age man with North African ancestry shows that contact occurred, though it left little mark. Only a minority of sampled Iberians carry steppe-related ancestry, so sampling per site matters.

populations.name: Chalcolithic Iberians with steppe-related ancestry
populations.description: A minority of Copper Age Iberians, labelled as genetic outliers in AADR, who carry steppe-related ancestry. They are the earliest detection of such ancestry in the peninsula.

membership.notes: Uses the AADR outlier label deliberately; the default outlier exclusion is overridden for this population.

caveats: Defined by an AADR outlier label; the exact correspondence to the 8 individuals of Olalde 2018 is not checked individual by individual.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are a minority of Copper Age Iberians marked as genetic outliers in the data because they carry steppe-related ancestry. The 2018 study found such ancestry in only 8 of 32 analysed Iberian Beaker-associated individuals, so most Beaker-associated people in Iberia did not have it. Four of the individuals with a steppe signal carry Y haplogroup R1b-M269.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: A later study reports the earliest evidence of steppe-related ancestry in the Bronze Age in 14 individuals dated about 2500-2000 BCE, who lived alongside local people without it. After 2000 BCE the groups admixed, producing a population with about 40% ancestry from incoming groups.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: This group is defined by an automatic outlier label rather than a checked list, and the match with the study's 8 individuals has not been confirmed one by one. The studies do not show where in Iberia the steppe-related ancestry was first acquired. The sample is small.

populations.name: Bronze Age people of Iberia
populations.description: Individuals from Bronze Age Iberia (about 2200–900 BCE). By about 2000 BCE a large share of their ancestry, and nearly all Y chromosomes, derive from people with steppe-related ancestry.

membership.notes: Grouped by region and period, not by a single genetic profile.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This panel groups Bronze Age people of Iberia, about 2200-900 BCE, by region and period, not by a single genetic profile. The 2019 study increased the Bronze Age dataset from 7 to 60 individuals. It shows steppe-related ancestry appearing throughout the peninsula, with less impact in the south. The groups are defined by region and period rather than by one shared genetic profile.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: By about 2000 BCE, about 40% of Iberia's ancestry came from incoming groups with steppe-related ancestry, as modelled in the study. The earliest 14 individuals, dated about 2500-2000 BCE, lived alongside local people who lacked it. The male Y-chromosome lineages changed far more than the genome overall, and lower non-local ancestry on the X chromosome points to more incoming males than females.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: In the same model the remaining roughly 60% came from the local Chalcolithic-related population. In the Iron Age, ancestry related to north and central Europe increased further, by 10-19% on the eastern coast, 11-31% in the southwest and 28-43% in the north. The authors link this to Late Bronze or early Iron Age gene flow.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The 40% figure and the male bias are inferred from model fits and the X-chromosome signal, not observed directly. The groups are defined by period and region, so the label covers varied local communities, and only 60 Bronze Age individuals represent about 1,300 years across a whole peninsula.

populations.name: Late Bronze Age and Iron Age people of southern Britain
populations.description: Individuals from England and Wales from the Late Bronze Age onward, whose ancestry shifted towards more early-farmer-related ancestry through migrants from the continent.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This panel groups people from England and Wales from the Late Bronze Age onward. They come from the 2022 Patterson study, which generated genome-wide data from 793 individuals and increased Middle to Late Bronze and Iron Age samples from Britain twelvefold. Sample sizes for Wales are too small for accurate inference, so the picture is mainly for England.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Ancestry from early European farmers rose in England and Wales: about 31% in the Copper Age/Early Bronze Age, 34.7% in the Middle Bronze Age, 36.1% in the Late Bronze Age and 37.9% in the Iron Age. There was no significant change in Scotland. Migrants most similar to ancient individuals from France contributed about half the ancestry of Iron Age people in England and Wales.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The farmer-related share was about 31% in the Copper Age and Early Bronze Age, before the rise. From about 2450 BCE, Beaker-associated migration had brought steppe-related ancestry to Britain. Later, migrants who arrived between 1000 and 875 BCE and over previous centuries contributed about half the ancestry of Iron Age people in England and Wales.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The source is a population best matched by ancient individuals from France, not a specific group, and the actual origin could lie elsewhere. The ancestry figures are model estimates with standard errors. Scotland shows no matching change, so the pattern is regional.

populations.name: Middle–Late Bronze Age steppe (Sintashta, Andronovo, Srubnaya-associated)
populations.description: People of the central Eurasian steppe in the 2nd millennium BCE associated with the Sintashta, Petrovka, Alakul/Andronovo and Srubnaya cultures. Ancestry with their profile reached South Asia via Central Asia.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This panel groups people of the central Eurasian steppe in the second millennium BCE, assigned to the Sintashta, Petrovka, Alakul-Andronovo and Srubnaya archaeological cultures. At Sintashta's Kamennyi Ambar V cemetery, 50 individuals include several outlier groups that were contemporaries of the main cluster but had different ancestry, which the authors read as a cosmopolitan site.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Steppe-related ancestry in these groups is modelled as about two thirds Yamnaya-related and about one third from the European Cline, a gradient of farmer and hunter-gatherer ancestry. The profile is shared by Corded Ware, Srubnaya, Petrovka and Sintashta groups. Another study finds the eastward steppe ancestry peaks near 70% in the earliest individuals and then declines, correlated with Globular Amphora-related ancestry. East Asian-related ancestry, up to about 25% in some individuals, becomes common later.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Yamnaya-related ancestry, mixed with ancestry from the European Cline, is the base of the profile these groups carry. Steppe-related ancestry with this profile reached South Asia via Central Asia after about 2000 BCE and contributed to people there called Ancestral North Indians. It has the same profile as in Bronze Age eastern Europe, and is modelled as arriving after the Indus Valley Civilization declined.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The panel combines several archaeological cultures, spread over many centuries and a very large area, so it hides regional differences. At Sintashta, outliers show people of varied ancestry living together, and a mean profile does not describe all of them. The 67/33 split is one published model. Groups with East Asian-related ancestry appear later in the steppe, so the profile changed over time.

populations.name: Botai-associated individuals
populations.description: People of northern Kazakhstan associated with the Botai culture, linked to the earliest evidence of horse husbandry, whose ancestry derives from hunter-gatherers deeply diverged from the Yamnaya.
caveats: Three individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Botai is an archaeological culture of northern Kazakhstan. It is linked to the earliest unambiguous evidence for horse husbandry, around 3500-3000 BCE. The study sequenced three Botai individuals from about 3500-3300 BCE, one at high coverage. Botai is a cultural label, so these three people stand in for a larger community that is mostly unsampled.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Botai derive from hunter-gatherers deeply diverged from Yamnaya. A coalescent model fits them as a mixture of ancient North Eurasian (ANE) ancestry, an old Siberian-linked lineage, and an Ancient East Asian component, with mixing around 5000 BCE. They show no Caucasus hunter-gatherer ancestry, and their Y chromosomes differ from those of Yamnaya males.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Botai ancestry continues the local hunter-gatherer population of Central Asia. The study found no gene flow with Yamnaya at a level different from zero, and the Botai and Yamnaya lineages are modelled as having diverged about 15,000 years ago. Central Asian hunter-gatherers persisted largely isolated after the Yamnaya and Afanasievo expansions.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only three individuals are sampled, so the sample may not capture variation in the wider community. Researchers disagree on whether Botai learned horse husbandry from western pastoralists or developed it themselves; the DNA fits local development but does not prove it. Model dates, such as the 15,000 years, are approximate.

populations.name: Indus Periphery Cline and the Rakhigarhi individual
populations.description: A genetic profile shared by one individual from an Indus Valley Civilization context (Rakhigarhi) and by outliers buried at sites in Iran and Turkmenistan that were in contact with the IVC: a mixture of ancient-Iranian-related and South Asian hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, with little or no steppe-related ancestry.

region.name: Northwest South Asia and its periphery

membership.notes: AADR v66.p1 does not label the 11 Indus Periphery outliers separately (they sit inside numbered clusters such as Turkmenistan_BA1-1 and Iran_ShahriSokhta_BA2-2); adding them needs the individual list from Narasimhan 2019.

caveats: Only one genome comes from an IVC context; whether it represents the IVC population as a whole is a hypothesis.
Membership is incomplete (see notes).

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Indus Periphery Cline is a genetic gradient seen in 11 outliers buried at Gonur in Turkmenistan and Shahr-i-Sokhta in eastern Iran, places in cultural contact with the Indus Valley Civilization (IVC). One genome from an IVC town, Rakhigarhi, matches it. Whether this profile was common in the IVC is a hypothesis, supported by circumstantial evidence, not a proven fact.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: People on the cline are modelled as a mix of two ends: ancestry related to Andamanese hunter-gatherers (11-50%), and a mix of Iranian farmer-related and West Siberian hunter-gatherer-related ancestry (about 50-89%). They show no detectable Anatolian farmer-related ancestry, and the Rakhigarhi genome has little or no steppe-related ancestry. The mixing is dated to about 5400-3700 BCE.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Indus Periphery-related ancestry makes up the majority of the ancestry of present-day South Asians and contributed to both Ancestral South Indians and Ancestral North Indians. Its Iranian-related part may not come from early Iranian farmers: Shinde and colleagues find it derives from a lineage that split before those groups separated. A proposed eastward spread of Iranian farmers is therefore contested.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only one genome comes from an IVC context, and 60 of 61 Rakhigarhi samples gave no usable DNA, so the IVC-wide pattern is unknown. The outliers lived outside the IVC heartland. Membership here is incomplete. Where and when the Iranian-related ancestry entered South Asia is open, with two rival explanations.

populations.name: Ancestral Ancient South Asians (AASI, modelled)
populations.description: A modelled ancestry component: the South Asian lineage with no relationship to West Eurasians, split around the time East Asian, Andamanese and Australian ancestors separated. No unmixed individual has been sampled.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: The time range is a display window, not a dated lifespan.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: AASI stands for Ancestral Ancient South Asians. It is a modelled ancestry component, not a sampled population: the South Asian lineage with no relationship to West Eurasians. No individual carrying only this ancestry has been sequenced. The dates on the timeline are a display window, not a lifespan.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In an admixture graph fitted to present-day groups, AASI is an Asian lineage that split around the time East Asian, Andaman Islander and Australian ancestors separated from each other. It is one end of the gradient that forms the main ancestry of South Asians, opposite Iranian-related ancestry. Andamanese hunter-gatherers serve as a stand-in for it in some models.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: AASI-related ancestry contributed to Ancestral South Indians and appears in the Indus Periphery profile, with 11-50% Andamanese hunter-gatherer-related ancestry in the 11 outliers. The Ancestral South Indians are modelled as at least 55% Indus Periphery-related, with the remainder AASI-related. A group like Juang needs extra AASI beyond that.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: AASI is a statistical reconstruction. It has no sampled members, and its age and location are unknown, so it should not be read as a people. Models of it rest on present-day South Asian groups and on Andamanese stand-ins. Alternative fits for the deep branching order may exist.

populations.name: Ancestral South Indians (ASI, modelled)
populations.description: A modelled ancestral population that formed after the decline of the Indus Valley Civilization as Indus Periphery-related people mixed with groups further southeast. It is one of the two main sources of ancestry in present-day South Asians.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: Display window; formation date is model-based.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: ASI stands for Ancestral South Indians. It is a modelled ancestral population, reconstructed statistically from ancient and present-day genomes: nobody from it has been sampled. It is one of the two main sources of ancestry in present-day South Asians. The dates shown are a display window, and the formation date is model-based.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The ASI are modelled as Indus Periphery-related people who mixed with groups further southeast that had more AASI-related ancestry. At least 55% of ASI ancestry is Indus Periphery-related and the rest AASI-related. Several southern Indian tribal groups sit at the extreme of the modern gradient and may be nearly direct descendants.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The mixing that formed the ASI is dated, in one present-day southern Indian group, to 1700-400 BCE, after the decline of the IVC. In parallel, Indus Periphery-related people mixed with steppe-related newcomers to form the ANI, and the ASI and ANI then mixed to form the gradient seen across present-day South Asia.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The ASI are inferred from modelling, not observed, and the date comes from one present-day group. The proportions depend on stand-in groups (Indus Periphery West and Andamanese hunter-gatherers). They describe ancestry, not a people, language or social group. Authors of the main study note that the ASI were not fully formed when the IVC existed.

populations.name: Ancestral North Indians (ANI, modelled)
populations.description: A modelled ancestral population that formed in the 2nd millennium BCE as Indus Periphery-related people mixed with people carrying steppe-related ancestry arriving via Central Asia.

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: Display window; formation date is model-based.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: ANI stands for Ancestral North Indians. It is a modelled ancestral population, one of the two main sources of ancestry in present-day South Asians. No one from it has been sampled. It formed in the 2nd millennium BCE as Indus Periphery-related people mixed with people carrying steppe-related ancestry who arrived via Central Asia. The dates here are a display window.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Steppe-related ancestry in South Asia has the same profile as that of Bronze Age eastern Europe. The authors model the 'Steppe Cline' of ancient individuals from the Swat Valley as running from a point on the Indus Periphery Cline to a mix of about 41% steppe ancestry (Central Steppe MLBA) and 59% Iranian-rich Indus Periphery ancestry. The ANI is statistically consistent with falling along this cline.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Steppe-related ancestry reached South Asia via Central Asia after about 2000 BCE, and the mixing is dated about 1900-1500 BCE in Swat. It mixed with Indus Periphery-related people, and then ANI and ASI mixed with each other. In Swat the steppe share was carried mostly by females, while the pattern in present-day groups is male-biased.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The ANI cannot be observed directly, and formation dates are model-based, with the Kalash estimate coming from a present-day group. Sex-bias results disagree between ancient Swat individuals and present-day groups. Later steppe groups with East Asian-related ancestry cannot be the main source, according to the authors. Sampling is concentrated on the Swat Valley.

populations.name: Jōmon-associated hunter-gatherers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherer-fishers of the Japanese archipelago associated with the Jōmon culture, whose ancestry belongs to a deeply splitting East Asian lineage.

membership.notes: Includes Initial to Final Jōmon individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Jomon is an archaeological culture of hunter-gatherer-fishers on the Japanese archipelago, known for pottery. This panel groups sampled individuals from the Initial to the Final Jomon, spanning several thousand years. The 2021 study sequenced nine Jomon individuals, and they share extremely high genetic drift with each other, forming a tight cluster. The authors read this as sustained geographic isolation.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Jomon-associated people belong to a deeply splitting East Asian lineage. One study models them as roughly 56% a southern Tianyuan-related lineage and 44% an Andaman Islander-related lineage. Another places a 2,500-year-old genome (IK002) basal to the East and Northeast Asian genomes examined, with affinity to indigenous Taiwanese people. These are model-based results from a few genomes.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: After the Jomon, Yayoi-period individuals show about half Jomon-related ancestry and half Northeast Asian-related ancestry, and Kofun-period individuals carry Jomon-related ancestry alongside Northeast Asian- and East Asian-related ancestry. Present-day Japanese ancestry includes about 15% Jomon-related ancestry in one model, with no further dilution since the Kofun period.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The routes of the earliest arrival are not shown by DNA alone: the coastal-route reading in two papers is the authors' interpretation, not a tested result. Japan's warm, humid climate and acidic soils generally preserve DNA poorly, so the sample is small, and one Final Jomon genome carries much of the lineage analysis. Proportions depend on the model chosen.

populations.name: Kofun-period individuals (Japan)
populations.description: Individuals from the Kofun period (about 300–700 CE), whose ancestry adds a large East Asian-related component to earlier Jōmon- and Yayoi-period ancestry.
caveats: Three individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are three individuals from the Kofun period, a time of state formation on the Japanese archipelago, dated about 1,300 years ago and treated here as a date-and-place grouping. They are the first genomic data from this period, and the comparison group of Yayoi individuals is only two people. They cluster with present-day Japanese in the study's analyses, and are genetically distinct from the earlier Yayoi-period individuals.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The best-fitting model for the Kofun individuals mixes three sources: Jomon-related, Northeast Asian-related and Han-related ancestry. Jomon ancestry is about four times lower than in the Yayoi individuals. Two-way models with the Yayoi plus a Han, Korean or Yellow River source give those sources 20-30% of Kofun ancestry. 'Han' here stands for broadly East Asian ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Jomon-related ancestry came first, then Northeast Asian-related ancestry in the Yayoi period, then East Asian-related ancestry in the Kofun period. The study finds that present-day Japanese carry the same three components in nearly the same proportions as the Kofun, with Jomon-related ancestry about 15% against 13% in the Kofun sample.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only three individuals are sampled, so the Kofun profile may not represent the whole archipelago. The authors favour two migration waves, but a single continuing source also fits some tests. 'Han' and 'Northeast Asian' are stand-in labels for sources. Only two Yayoi genomes are available to compare against.

populations.name: Amur River basin hunter-gatherers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of the Amur River basin, whose ancestry stayed remarkably stable over thousands of years.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This group holds hunter-gatherers of the Amur River basin in northeastern Asia, including 18 people from the Boisman-2 cemetery of about 5400-3600 BCE and two Early Neolithic individuals of about 5525-5320 BCE. Several later individuals of the Iron Age and Xianbei period also fit the same cluster. The Amur people kept hunting, fishing and some cultivation into the historic era.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Amur individuals form one genetic cluster from about 5500 BCE to the Xianbei period, with no substantial change in their affinity to outside populations. They share a deeply splitting lineage with Jomon-associated people, and they are modelled as roughly 87% Mongolian Neolithic-related and 13% Jomon-related. Ancestry stayed stable while the Yellow River and West Liao River changed.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Amur-related ancestry contributed to the Bronze Age West Liao River, coinciding with pastoralism, and to later groups: a Heishui Mohe individual from about 1100 CE carries about 43% Amur Neolithic ancestry. The cluster fits within the range of present-day Amur populations, though a strict-continuity test rejects the ancient group as their direct ancestors.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The sample is small, with the Early Neolithic represented by two people and later periods by a handful. The authors treat the 21% West Liao River result as speculation. 'Stable' describes affinity to outside groups, not the absence of local mixing, since the continuity test with present-day groups fails.

populations.name: Yellow River basin Neolithic farmers
populations.description: Millet farmers of the middle and lower Yellow River basin in the Neolithic, whose ancestry later contributed widely in East Asia, including to Tibetan groups and Han Chinese.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This group is millet farmers of the middle and lower Yellow River basin in the Neolithic, mainly from sites of the Yangshao culture (about 3550-3050 BCE) and the Longshan culture (about 2275-1844 BCE). The 2020 study sampled the region at ten sites between 3550 and 50 BCE. Crop cultivation was already the main subsistence strategy there by the Middle Neolithic.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Yellow River farmers form a distinct genetic cluster. Late Neolithic individuals are closer to present-day southern Chinese and Southeast Asians than Middle Neolithic ones, which the authors link to a possible northward spread of rice farming. Another study infers that a northern Tianyuan-related lineage gave about 90% of the ancestry of Upper Yellow River Neolithic farmers.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Yellow River farmer-related ancestry (around 3000 BCE) contributed up to about 84% to some Tibetan groups and about 59-84% to Han Chinese, with the rest from a southern source. It also reached the West Liao River region and Inner Mongolia: groups there are modelled as about 80% Yellow River farmers. These are present-day links inferred from modern genomes.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Candidate sources of the southern ancestry, such as Shandong and lower Yangtze populations, are unsampled, so the rice-farming link is a hypothesis. The Middle Neolithic Yangshao sample is only eight individuals. For Tibetans, other models also marginally fit, because the genetic data lack fine resolution.

populations.name: West Liao River basin Neolithic and Bronze Age people
populations.description: Individuals from the West Liao River region of northeast China, whose ancestry shifted over time, towards the Yellow River with intensifying farming and towards the Amur with Bronze Age pastoralism.

membership.notes: Grouped by region; not a single genetic profile.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This panel groups people from the West Liao River region of northeast China, from the Middle Neolithic (Hongshan culture, about 3550-3050 BCE) to the Bronze Age (Upper Xiajiadian culture, about 1050-350 BCE). It is a geographic grouping and not a single genetic profile. The region lies between the Yellow River and the Amur River, and millet was cultivated there from at least 6000 BCE, with reliance on it changing over time.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The ancestry changed through time. Middle Neolithic groups fall between Amur and Yellow River profiles, with 40-75% Amur-related ancestry. Late Neolithic groups are modelled as 74-88% Yellow River-related. A second study models West Liao River farmers as about 67% Upper Yellow River-related and 33% southern Liangdao-related. Bronze Age groups shift back toward Amur-related ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Late Neolithic farming intensification coincides with increased Yellow River affinity, and Bronze Age pastoralism with increased Amur affinity. Two Bronze Age individuals are modelled as 21% from an Amur-related person, which the authors suggest may mean recent migration into the region.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The groups are small, and the Bronze Age sample is a few people. A correlation between subsistence change and ancestry change does not show cause. The authors say the Middle Neolithic geographic mixing may have continued but that the data cannot test it. One study finds the West Liao River farmer mixture absent from the Mongolian and Amur time series.

populations.name: Iron Age people of Taiwan
populations.description: Individuals from Taiwan (about 1300 BCE–800 CE) carrying mostly southern East Asian ancestry, with a smaller northern component. Their ancestry resembles that of Austronesian-related groups in the cited studies; no claim about language is made here.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are individuals from two sites in Taiwan dated about 1300 BCE-800 CE. The 2021 study sequenced 46 of them. Their Y chromosomes and maternal lineages are shared with present-day Indigenous Taiwanese people, and with ancient individuals from Vanuatu. The label groups burials by place and date. It does not name a single people.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: About 75% of their ancestry is modelled as coming from a southern lineage, likely related to Yangtze River farmers, which is also common in several present-day groups of southern East Asia and Southeast Asia. About 25% comes from a northern lineage related to but different from Yellow River farmers. The southern farmers themselves have not been sampled.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: A northern source contributed ancestry to the Taiwan farmers. It does not fit Yellow River farmers themselves, and so the authors infer an additional north-to-south movement. Another study sees Northern East Asian ancestry spreading across southern East Asia after the Neolithic, and finds Neolithic southern and Taiwan Strait individuals connected with Austronesian-related ancestry. Jomon-associated people share a deeply splitting lineage.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The southern farmer source is inferred, because no ancient Yangtze farmers have been sampled. The millet link for the northern ancestry is a speculation by the authors. One related study is read from its abstract only, so its details are unchecked. Forty-six individuals from two sites stand in for 2,000 years of Taiwan's history.

populations.name: Hòabìnhian-associated hunter-gatherers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of mainland Southeast Asia associated with the Hòabìnhian technocomplex, whose deeply diverged eastern Eurasian ancestry contributed to later Southeast Asians.
caveats: Two individuals; claims verified against the abstract only.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Hoabinhian is an archaeological technocomplex of hunter-gatherers in mainland Southeast Asia. This panel groups sampled individuals with Hoabinhian context, of which very few are sampled. One is an 8,000-year-old individual from Laos. The main study of these genomes found both Hoabinhian-related and East Asian farmer-related ancestry in present-day Southeast Asians.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Hoabinhian-related ancestry contributed to Southeast Asian diversity alongside East Asian farmer-related ancestry. Neolithic farmers of northern Vietnam carried both southern Chinese farmer-related and local hunter-gatherer-related ancestry. A Jomon-context genome sits in PCA between present-day East Asians and a cluster of ancient Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers and the 40,000-year-old Tianyuan individual, and an earlier report finds affinity with an 8,000-year-old Hoabinhian from Laos.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Details here rest on the abstract of the main study, since its full text is not openly available, so sample sizes and models are not checked. Only two individuals are in the data used, from two sites. The affinity with the Jomon-context genome comes from a different study that cites it, so it is secondhand.

populations.name: Neolithic farmers of mainland Southeast Asia (Man Bac)
populations.description: Early farmers of northern Vietnam, about 4,000 years ago, whose ancestry combines southern East Asian farmer-related and local hunter-gatherer-related components.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are early farmers buried at Man Bac in northern Vietnam about 4,000 years ago (4100-3600 years ago). The 2018 study sampled eight individuals from the site as part of 18 from five sites in Southeast Asia. Preservation in tropical conditions was poor, so each genome has limited coverage.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Man Bac farmers mix two sources: East Asian ancestry related to southern Chinese farmers and ancestry from deeply diverged eastern Eurasian hunter-gatherers. In one model the proportions are about 70% farmer-related and 30% hunter-gatherer-related, shared with present-day Nicobarese and Mlabri. One individual, VN29, has more local hunter-gatherer ancestry, which the authors read as recent contact between farmers and hunter-gatherers.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Hoabinhian-related ancestry contributed to Southeast Asian diversity alongside East Asian farmer-related ancestry. By the Bronze Age, individuals at Vietnamese and Myanmar sites look closer to present-day majority groups, reflecting additional influxes of migrants. Farmers at Ban Chiang in Thailand and Vat Komnou in Cambodia cluster with Man Bac in the first analysis, while Bronze Age Nui Nap in Vietnam projects close to present-day Vietnamese.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Eight individuals from one site represent the group. The ancestry proportions come from a model fitted with present-day populations, which may not describe ancient ones. Poor preservation means low coverage. The authors link these ancestries to language families, and that interpretation is not shown here.

populations.name: Xiongnu-period individuals (Mongolia)
populations.description: People of the Eastern Steppe during the time of the Xiongnu polity (about 200 BCE–100 CE), whose ancestry reflects mixing of earlier Mongolian and surrounding populations.
caveats: 'Xiongnu-period' is a date-and-place grouping; it does not imply a single ethnic identity.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are 60 people buried in Mongolia during the period of the Xiongnu polity, roughly 200 BCE-100 CE, the first empire founded by pastoralists. The label is a date-and-place grouping. It does not imply a single ethnic identity. The earliest burials come mostly from northern frontier sites, while most later burials date after 50 BCE.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Xiongnu-period individuals formed from mixing between earlier Mongolian populations and surrounding groups. Early on, half cluster with an Altai-Sayan group of the Early Iron Age, while others mix that group with Ulaanzuukh Slab Grave ancestry. Late Xiongnu are more varied: some resemble Sarmatian-related steppe groups, and some mix with Han-related ancestry. The period united the gene pools of western and eastern Mongolia.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: A pastoralist expansion reached Mongolia around 3000 BCE, and by the Late Bronze Age three structured groups all practised dairy pastoralism regardless of ancestry. After the Xiongnu empire, Early Medieval individuals show genetic profiles that differ from the Xiongnu period, suggesting new gene flow, and Mongol-period individuals show much higher eastern Eurasian ancestry.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Xiongnu panel is a date-and-place grouping of burials, so ancestry should not be read as political or ethnic membership. Sampling is uneven across sites, with only 13 early individuals, mostly from northern frontier sites. Model sources such as Chandman_IA, Sarmatian, BMAC and Han are proxies for unsampled groups.

populations.name: Mongol-period individuals (Mongolia)
populations.description: People of Mongolia during the Mongol Empire era (about 1200–1400 CE), with much higher eastern Eurasian ancestry than in the Xiongnu period.

membership.notes: AADR uses 'LateMedieval' for the Mongol period.

caveats: A date-and-place grouping, not an ethnic identity.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are people buried in Mongolia during the Mongol Empire, about 1200-1400 CE, grouped by date and place only. The 2020 study analysed 62 such individuals. Their burials are consistent with low-level local elites, so the sample excludes royal burials and the capital city of Karakorum. The label does not imply an ethnic identity.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Mongol-period individuals show much higher eastern Eurasian ancestry than in the Xiongnu period. As a group they fit a three-way model: 55-64% Ulaanzuukh Slab Grave ancestry, 21-27% Han-related ancestry and 15-18% Western Steppe ancestry, explaining 56 of 61 individuals. They are less genetically varied than the Xiongnu-era people.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Mongol-period ancestry follows the mixed Xiongnu and Early Medieval periods and almost lacks the residual ancient North Eurasian-related ancestry carried by the Xiongnu and earlier northern groups. The authors say this period marks the beginning of the modern Mongolian gene pool, which resembles present-day Mongolic-speaking populations.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The sample is of local elites, so it may not represent commoners or royals. The three source labels are stand-ins, and five individuals do not fit the model. The link to present-day populations comes from comparing modern genomes, so it is an inference and not a direct line of descent.

populations.name: Founding population of Native Americans (inferred)
populations.description: A modelled population: the shared ancestors of Ancient Beringians and all other Native Americans, which separated from East Asian-related populations, received gene flow related to Ancient North Eurasians, and later branched. Its location during this time is not known from genetics.

region.name: Northeast Asia / Beringia (not located by genetics)

membership.notes: Inferred only.

caveats: The window spans the modelled split from East Asians (~36,000 years ago) to the divergence of northern and southern branches (~14,600 years ago, lower bound) in Moreno-Mayar 2018 (abstract only); other studies place the founding migration later (no earlier than 23,000 years ago, Raghavan 2015).

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This is a modelled population, not a sampled one. It stands for the shared ancestors of Ancient Beringians and all other Native Americans, after they separated from East Asian-related populations and received ancestry related to Ancient North Eurasians. Genetics does not locate where these ancestors lived. The group is inferred from the ancient genomes of Upward Sun River, Anzick-1 and later Americans.

overview.heading: When and where
overview.text: Dates differ between models. One model has the split from East Asians about 36,000 years ago and branching of the northern and southern Native American lines 17,500-14,600 years ago. Another places the split about 30,000 years ago. Raghavan and colleagues find a single migration wave from Siberia no earlier than 23,000 years ago. Where the ancestors lived is not known from genetics.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The founders are modelled as East Asian-related ancestry plus a share related to Ancient North Eurasians such as the Mal'ta individual, estimated at 14-38% of Native American ancestry in one study. This mixing happened before the northern and southern branches diverged. Native Americans diversified into two basal branches around 13,000 years ago in another analysis.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The models disagree on dates and on where branching happened: eastern Beringia or lower-latitude North America. The 36,000-year figure rests on an abstract-only reading of one paper. These ancestors are a ghost population: nobody from this stage has been sequenced. Later gene flow also complicates the picture.

populations.name: Ancient Beringians (Upward Sun River)
populations.description: Two infants buried at Upward Sun River, Alaska, about 11,500 years ago, representing a population basal to all other Native Americans.
caveats: Claims verified against the abstract only.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Ancient Beringians are known from infants buried at Upward Sun River in interior Alaska about 11,500 years ago. Their genome (USR1) is basal to all other Native Americans: it branches off before those lineages separated from each other. The group is defined by two infants at a single site.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In one model, Ancient Beringians branched from the founding Native American population about 22,000-18,000 years ago. Another model finds that ancient Siberian ancestry related to the Ancient North Siberians (Yana) contributed about 18% (95% CI 9.8-20.3) to USR1. The two models give different dates.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only two infants from one site represent the group. Claims about the group rely on an abstract-only reading of the main paper. Where the split took place is uncertain: one study suggests eastern Beringia, another lower-latitude North America. The 22,000-18,000-year branching is the output of one model.

populations.name: Anzick-1 (Clovis-associated)
populations.description: An infant buried with Clovis tools in Montana about 12,600 years ago, more closely related to all Indigenous Americans than to any other population.
caveats: A single individual.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Anzick-1 is an infant boy buried with Clovis stone tools and red ochre at the Anzick site in Montana about 12,600 years ago. He is the only known Clovis burial. His genome was sequenced to 14.4x coverage. The remains are those of a single individual, so he cannot represent everyone who used Clovis tools.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Anzick-1 is more closely related to all Indigenous Americans than to any other group, and shares the ancient North Eurasian-related ancestry that entered Native American ancestors before about 12,600 years ago. He has less shared history with northern groups in Canada and the Arctic than with Central and South Americans. The data fit his belonging to a population ancestral to many present-day Native Americans.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Structure between northern and southern Native American lineages predates Anzick-1. His relatedness is greatest in Central and South Americans, and the oldest individuals from Chile, Brazil and Belize share an affinity with him that later South Americans lack. This links the Clovis-associated genome to some early Central and South Americans.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: A single infant cannot show how varied Clovis-associated people were. The affinity of early South Americans to Anzick-1 does not by itself show that Clovis people moved south, and Posth and colleagues say other scenarios also fit. Several different branching scenarios are compatible with the data.

populations.name: Early Holocene people of Central and South America
populations.description: The oldest sampled individuals from Belize, Brazil, Chile, Peru and Argentina (before about 8,000 years ago). Some of the earliest share an affinity with Anzick-1 that is absent in later South Americans.

membership.notes: Grouped by region and date: these individuals do not form one genetic cluster.

caveats: AADR labels for early Belize individuals contain 'Archaic_Maya', projecting a much later identity back in time; we keep the label as data only.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This panel groups the oldest sampled people of Belize, Brazil, Chile, Peru and Argentina, from before about 8,000 years ago, by region and date only. They do not form one genetic cluster. The 2018 study reports 49 individuals in four time series, each starting 10,900-8,600 years ago. Data labels from Belize contain a later cultural name that we keep as data only.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The oldest individuals show little specific allele sharing with present-day people. Nine ancient groups fit as a star-like radiation from one source population on the southern Native American branch, with the order of early lineages unresolved. Some of the earliest, at Los Rieles in Chile and Lapa do Santo in Brazil, share more alleles with Anzick-1 than later South Americans do.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Central and South Americans radiated rapidly from one of the two early Native American branches. Later South Americans derive from lineages without a specific Clovis affinity, which the authors read as a population replacement beginning at least 9,000 years ago followed by regional continuity; no single proportion is given. A second stream of gene flow reached the Central Andes by about 4,200 years ago.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Anzick-1 link can be read in two ways: movement out of North America after Clovis, or an earlier, pre-Clovis arrival of non-Anzick ancestry. No ancient individual shows the Australasian-related signal found in some present-day Amazonian groups. The groups are small and span thousands of kilometres, so they should not be read as a single people.

populations.name: People of the Central and South-Central Andes
populations.description: Individuals from the Andean highlands and Pacific coast of Peru and Bolivia over the last 9,000 years, among whom present-day Andean genetic structure began forming by about 5,800 years ago.

membership.notes: Grouped by region.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This panel groups people from the Andean highlands and Pacific coast of Peru and Bolivia over the last 9,000 years by region. The 2020 study reports 89 individuals dated 9,000-500 years ago from many cultural contexts, including Wari, Tiwanaku, Moche and Inca sites. It does not describe one population but a region's changing communities.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Present-day Andean genetic structure began forming by about 5,800 years ago: northern and southern highland lineages had separated by then, with gene flow between highlands and coast afterwards. The oldest Peruvian individuals, about 9,000 years old, share most with present-day Indigenous groups of the Central Andes. After about 2,000 years ago, regions stayed genetically homogeneous.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: A stream of gene flow with an affinity to ancient individuals of the California Channel Islands reached the Central Andes by about 4,200 years ago. Between 2,000 and 500 years ago neighbouring groups show minimal admixture, but Tiwanaku and the Inca heartland were cosmopolitan: people of diverse ancestries lived side by side. Present-day groups resemble ancient individuals of their region.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The panel combines regions that differ genetically, so one average would mislead. Sampling is uneven: the oldest highland people are few. Gene flow directions between North and South Highlands could not be determined. The match between ancient and present-day groups concerns genetics only, not language or identity. The reason Cusco individuals differ from present-day Cusco people is an open question.

populations.name: Archaic Age people of the Caribbean
populations.description: The Caribbean's first inhabitants, before the Ceramic Age, descended from a deeply divergent population closest to Central and northern South Americans.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Archaic Age people were the first inhabitants of the Caribbean, before the Ceramic Age. The Caribbean was first settled about 6,000 years ago. The 2021 study analysed 50 Archaic-associated individuals from Cuba, dated about 3,200-700 years ago, plus one from the Dominican Republic. Effective population sizes were small, about 200-300.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Archaic Age Caribbean people derive from a deeply divergent population closest to Central and northern South Americans. They show no excess sharing with Mesoamerican or North American groups, and the study found no support for earlier claims of ancestry from a population related to North Americans. Archaic individuals in Cuba share more with each other than with the Dominican individual.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Most Archaic ancestry was displaced when ceramic users arrived: Archaic lineages were more than 98% replaced by a homogeneous ceramic-using population in much of the Caribbean. An exception is western Cuba, where Archaic lineages persisted with minimal mixture for over 2,500 years.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Most Archaic genomes come from Cuba, so other islands are thinly sampled and one Dominican individual stands for Hispaniola. Closeness to Central and northern South Americans does not locate the origin. Population sizes are estimates from genetic data with wide ranges.

populations.name: Ceramic Age people of the Caribbean
populations.description: Ceramic-using people of the Caribbean from at least 1,700 years ago, genetically homogeneous and related to groups of northeastern South America (the link to Arawak-related groups depends on the method used). Their arrival almost entirely replaced Archaic Age ancestry in the islands sampled.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Ceramic Age people were the pottery-making farmers of the Caribbean from at least 1,700 years ago. The 2021 study analysed 194 individuals dated about 1,700-400 years ago from the Bahamas, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico and Cuba. They were genetically homogeneous, with effective population size of about 500-1,500 and 19 pairs of cross-island cousins.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Ceramic Age people carry almost none of the earlier Archaic ancestry: about 0.5-2.0% overall, with three individuals in Hispaniola at 11.8-18.5%. They fit a source like the Lesser Antilles ceramic population, which spread south to north. Admixture analysis suggests an Arawak affinity, but another test does not show Arawak speakers closer than Cariban or Tupian ones.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Archaic Age lineages were more than 98% replaced by this population in much of the Caribbean. Pottery-style changes within the Ceramic Age were not driven by migration of genetically distinct groups. Present-day Puerto Ricans show relatedness to Ceramic-associated individuals in two datasets, an inference from modern genomes.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Arawak connection depends on the method used, and the proxies may not match the real source. The study could not detect a Carib migration contributing under 2-8%. Estimates of population size are lower bounds from genetic data. The Venezuelan sample is eight individuals.

populations.name: Ancestors of Papuans and Aboriginal Australians (inferred)
populations.description: A modelled population: the ancestors of present-day Papuans and Aboriginal Australians, who carry more Denisovan-related ancestry than other non-Africans. No ancient genome from this population falls in the V1 window.

region.name: Island Southeast Asia and Sahul (not located by genetics)

membership.notes: Inferred from present-day genomes.

caveats: Display window only: the cited sources do not date this population.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This is a modelled population: the ancestors of present-day Papuans and Aboriginal Australians, inferred from present-day genomes. They carry more Denisovan-related ancestry than other non-Africans. No ancient genome from this population falls in the V1 window, and the dates shown are a display window only. Genetics does not locate them.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Aboriginal Australians and Papuans carry more Denisovan-derived haplotypes than other non-Africans. The first estimate, in 2010, put Denisovan-related ancestry at 4-6% of present-day Melanesian genomes. A Denisovan pulse is modelled at 31-50 thousand years ago, and the haplotype count tracks the Australo-Papuan share of ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Papuan and Aboriginal Australian ancestors diversified 25-40 thousand years ago and diverged from Eurasians 51-72 thousand years ago in the model. Papuan-related ancestry later spread to Remote Oceania, where present-day groups carry at least 25% of it. Separate Denisovan admixture is also proposed for Philippine Ayta Magbukon, who carry more Denisovan ancestry than Papuans.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: All estimates come from present-day genomes and models, so dates have wide intervals. One model finds two out-of-Africa waves and another, which includes archaic admixture, finds one. The 4-6% Denisovan figure is a first estimate. The group has no sampled members.

populations.name: First Remote Oceanians (Lapita-associated)
populations.description: The first people to settle Vanuatu and Tonga, about 3,000 years ago, buried with Lapita material. Their ancestry was almost entirely East Asian-related, with little or no Papuan-related ancestry.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are the first people to settle Remote Oceania, buried with Lapita material at Teouma on Efate in Vanuatu (about 3,100-2,700 years ago) and Talasiu on Tongatapu in Tonga (about 2,700-2,300 years ago). The 2016 study sequenced four individuals, all female. They cluster tightly together and are not shifted toward Papuan ancestry.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Their ancestry was almost entirely East Asian-related, with little or no Papuan-related ancestry. They resemble the Taiwanese Ami and Atayal in PCA, unlike present-day Remote Oceanians, and fit descent from the population that spread from Taiwan via the Philippines to western Melanesia from about 5,000 years ago, with minimal mixing along the way. The East Asian-related ancestry they carry no longer exists unmixed today.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Because present-day Pacific peoples carry at least 25% Papuan-related ancestry, that ancestry must have spread after first settlement. In Vanuatu, a dramatic turnover is apparent after about 2,900 and before about 2,300 years ago, when people of almost entirely Papuan-related ancestry arrived. The Lapita-related ancestry later declined to a minor share.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Four female individuals from two sites represent the group, so they may not reflect everyone in the first settlement or the full range of ancestry among its members. The source population, which no longer exists unmixed, is known through stand-ins such as the Taiwanese Ami.

populations.name: Post-Lapita people of Vanuatu
populations.description: People of Vanuatu from about 2,300 years ago onward, whose ancestry is predominantly Papuan-related after centuries of mixing with the first Lapita-associated settlers.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are people of Vanuatu from about 2,300 years ago onward, grouped by place and date. Their ancestry is mostly Papuan-related. The Lipson study sampled 14 ancient individuals from Efate and Epi, and the Posth study 19 individuals across the South Pacific. The arrival likely began a few centuries earlier, at the end of the Lapita period, when skeletal forms changed and long-distance trade between Near and Remote Oceania ended.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: People of almost entirely Papuan-related ancestry reached Vanuatu by about 2,300 years ago. Papuan-related ancestry later declined through mixing but remains at least 80-90% on most islands. Malakula individuals from 2,500 BP carry 22-46% Austronesian-related ancestry, showing the mixing took place over centuries, with sex-biased admixture.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: A Papuan-related expansion into Remote Oceania began about 2,500 years ago and led to near-complete replacement of Lapita-related ancestry in Vanuatu; Papuan-related ancestry is still at least 80-90% on most islands. It came from the Bismarck Archipelago. Present-day South Pacific populations carry at least 25% Papuan-related ancestry, which must have spread after first settlement.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The two studies differ: one reads a single large arrival by about 2,300 years ago, the other an incremental process of repeated movements from 2,500 years ago. Present-day Vanuatu includes a component absent from the ancient samples. The ancient samples are few and from a handful of islands, so local histories differ.

populations.name: Bismarck Archipelago-related ancestry (source, inferred)
populations.description: The source of the Papuan-related ancestry that reached Vanuatu, best matched by present-day people of the Bismarck Archipelago. No ancient individual from the source has been sampled.

membership.notes: Inferred from present-day genomes.

location_hint.label: Bismarck Archipelago (region named in the source)

caveats: Display window spans the arrival of Papuan-related ancestry in Vanuatu, not a lifespan.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This is an inferred source, not a sampled group: the population that gave the Papuan-related ancestry that reached Vanuatu. It is best matched by present-day people of the Bismarck Archipelago, such as the Baining of New Britain. No ancient individual from it has been sampled, and the dates shown are a display window.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: A detailed analysis finds that the Papuan-related ancestry in Vanuatu comes from the Bismarck Archipelago and not from the nearer Solomon Islands. The earliest post-Lapita individual in Vanuatu is modelled as descended from a population ancestral to present-day Baining Marabu, with affinity not explained by shared Austronesian ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Bismarck Archipelago-related ancestry arrived in Vanuatu by about 2,300 years ago and contributed most of the ancestry of post-Lapita people there. The Papuan-related ancestry in Polynesia derives from different sources, a third stream. These later movements changed the ancestry of the first Remote Oceanians' descendants.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Present-day Baining are stand-ins for an unsampled ancient source, whose real location and population are uncertain. The earliest individual's affinity to Baining spans a very large distance. Only a few ancient Vanuatu individuals test the link, and it does not say how the movement took place.

populations.name: Mota (Ethiopia)
populations.description: A man who lived about 4,500 years ago in the Ethiopian highlands, whose genome predates the Eurasian-related admixture found in many present-day eastern Africans.
caveats: The source paper carries an erratum; only claims unaffected by it are used.
A single individual.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: Mota is a single man who lived about 4,500 years ago in the Ethiopian highlands, buried in Mota Cave. His high-coverage genome serves as a reference for eastern African ancestry from before the Eurasian-related mixing seen in many present-day eastern Africans. The original paper was corrected in 2016 after a processing error; only claims unaffected by the correction are used here.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: In the 2022 study of ancient African foragers, Mota sits at the northern end of a north-south gradient of ancestry. He is modelled with about 30% of a separate, deeply diverged ancestry with no sampled relatives, called a ghost component. Other studies use his genome as a stand-in for northeastern African forager ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Mota-related ancestry appears in later eastern Africans. Present-day Hadza can be modelled as deriving all their ancestry from a lineage related to him, and Pastoral Neolithic herders carry about 20% Mota-related ancestry alongside Levantine- and Dinka-related ancestry. These are proxy relationships and do not show that Mota's own community was ancestral.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only one individual is sampled, so his genome may not represent other people of that time and region. The ghost ancestry is inferred and has no sampled relatives. Details of the original paper rest on its abstract and the erratum abstract, since the full text is not open access.

populations.name: Eastern African foragers
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of eastern Africa over the last 18,000 years, carrying a deep eastern African lineage. Their ancestry later mixed with incoming herders and farmers.
caveats: Few individuals across a very large area and time span.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are hunter-gatherers of eastern Africa (mainly Kenya and Tanzania) over the last 18,000 years, mostly buried at rockshelters and caves. The 2022 study reports six new individuals from Tanzania, Malawi and Zambia and re-analyses 28 others. Samples are few and thinly spread over a very large area and time span, and the new genomes have a median coverage of only 0.06x.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Eastern African forager ancestry is modelled as a mix of three highly divergent sources: a deep eastern African lineage (Mota-related), a deep southern African lineage, and a component most common today in central African rainforest foragers. In western Kenya the shares are about 62%, 19% and 19%; in north-central Tanzania about 54%, 12% and 34%.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Southern African-related ancestry reached farther north than today: a forager on Zanzibar about 1,400 years ago has about 31% of it. Later, the first herders of Kenya and Tanzania formed through mixing between northeastern African-related peoples and eastern African foragers. Gene flow was imbalanced, with forager ancestry entering herder groups but little flowing the other way.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Mota-related and southern African-related sources have no closely related sampled groups, so they are inferred. The clusters are based on few individuals with low coverage. Foragers lived on until at least 400 years ago beside herders and farmers, so the group is not a single period or place. Near lakes and coasts foragers show little herder admixture, while the Kakapel forager carries Mbuti-associated ancestry, so local histories differ.

populations.name: Foragers of Malawi
populations.description: Hunter-gatherers of Malawi between about 15,000 and 2,500 years ago, about two-thirds of whose ancestry is related to that of present-day southern African San.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are hunter-gatherers buried at rockshelters in Malawi, including Hora 1, Fingira and Chencherere, between about 15,000 and 2,500 years ago. The 2017 study found no significant genetic heterogeneity among seven Malawi individuals spanning about 8,100-2,500 years, which suggests one distinctive population that lasted at least 5,000 years.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: About two thirds of their ancestry is related to that of present-day southern African San: about 60% at Fingira about 6,100 years ago and about 65% about 2,500 years ago. Their ancestry is also modelled, with that of other eastern and south-central foragers, as a mix of three highly divergent sources.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: San-related ancestry was once much more widespread than today, reaching Malawi and Tanzania. Mitochondrial lineages of Malawi and Zambia foragers are mostly associated with southern African foragers, though a 16,000-year-old Hora 1 individual carries an eastern-African-associated one. After the spread of farmers from western Africa, local hunter-gatherer ancestry is barely detected in Malawi, a near-complete turnover.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Malawi sample is a few individuals from a handful of rockshelters over thousands of years. The studies model the southern African-related ancestry with present-day San as a proxy, and it may be only distantly related to them. Small differences exist between individuals in Malawi and Zambia.

populations.name: Southern African foragers
populations.description: Stone Age hunter-gatherers of southern Africa, genetically similar to present-day southern San groups.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are Stone Age hunter-gatherers of southern Africa, mainly from South Africa about 2,000 years ago, whose ancestry resembles that of present-day southern San groups. They include three individuals from KwaZulu-Natal (reported by Schlebusch and colleagues) and two from western Cape burials of about 2,000 years ago (Skoglund and colleagues). Only a handful of people represent the region, and the Schlebusch study of the KwaZulu-Natal individuals is read from its abstract only.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Ancient southern African ancestry makes up up to 91% of the ancestry of Khoe-San groups today. Two individuals from hunter-gatherer contexts about 2,000 years ago share ancestry with Khoe-San, the present-day southern African groups. The three KwaZulu-Natal individuals of about 2,000 years ago also resemble present-day southern San, whereas Iron Age individuals there resemble present-day Bantu-language speakers.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: San-related ancestry once reached far to the north and east, making up about two thirds of the ancestry of Malawi hunter-gatherers. In later centuries, ancestry from eastern African herders reached southern Africa: a pastoralist of about 1,200 years ago has about 40% of it, and Iron Age Botswana individuals carry 10-40% southern African hunter-gatherer ancestry alongside ancestry related to present-day Bantu speakers.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only a few individuals are sampled, and one study is read from its abstract. Present-day San groups are used as proxies, but all of them also carry ancestry from later herders and farmers, so they are an imperfect guide. How the ancestry was spread across southern Africa before 2,000 years ago is not known.

populations.name: Shum Laka individuals (Cameroon)
populations.description: Children buried at the Shum Laka rock shelter in Cameroon about 8,000 and 3,000 years ago, with ancestry most similar to west-central African hunter-gatherers.
caveats: Four individuals.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: These are four children buried at the Shum Laka rock shelter in the Grassfields of western Cameroon, two about 8,000 years ago and two about 3,000 years ago. Within each pair the children were close relatives, which supports the idea that the shelter was used as a family cemetery. All four show signs of recent inbreeding. The males carry Y haplogroups B and the rare A00.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: The children are most similar to present-day West-Central African hunter-gatherers. In one model they are about 35% West-Central African hunter-gatherer-related and about 65% from a lineage that split off early within West Africans. The later pair has about 5% more hunter-gatherer-related ancestry than the earlier pair.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: Present-day western Cameroonians and Bantu speakers are not substantially descended from the Shum Laka population. Present-day groups near the site, such as Mbo, Aghem and Bafut, show only small Shum Laka-related admixture, at most about 7-8%. The authors conclude that the population these four children represent did not contribute substantially to present-day western Cameroonians or to Bantu speakers across Africa.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: Only four children, all close relatives within pairs, are sampled, so they cannot represent a whole population. The models use ghost lineages without sampled representatives, and a less simple model also fits. Ancestry is inferred partly from present-day proxies and the split dates are approximate.

populations.name: Pastoral Neolithic herders of eastern Africa
populations.description: The first herders of Kenya and Tanzania, about 5,000–1,200 years ago, formed by mixing between northeastern African-related peoples and local foragers. Makers of different Pastoral Neolithic artefact traditions were not genetically distinct.

membership.notes: Tanzania_3000BP is the Luxmanda individual (Skoglund 2017).

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: The Pastoral Neolithic herders were the first herders of Kenya and Tanzania, from about 5,000 to 1,200 years ago. The 2019 study sequenced 31 early pastoral and Pastoral Neolithic individuals. They form a tight genetic cluster, even though their material culture differs: makers of different artefact traditions, such as Elmenteitan and Savanna Pastoral Neolithic, were not genetically distinct.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: They are modelled as a mix of three sources: roughly 40% Dinka-related, 40% Levantine-related and 20% Mota-related ancestry. A 3,100-year-old pastoralist from Luxmanda is modelled with 38% (plus or minus 1) Levantine pre-pottery farmer-related ancestry. Kenyan Pastoral Neolithic individuals vary in their forager and Dinka-related shares, e.g. 33% (plus or minus 11) Dinka-related at Hyrax Hill.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The herder groups formed through admixture between northeastern African-related peoples and eastern African foragers, according to the 2019 study. Later admixture with northeastern and western African-related groups appears by the Iron Age. Luxmanda-related pastoralist ancestry also appears in southern Africa by about 1,200 years ago.

overview.heading: What we cannot tell
overview.text: The Levantine-related ancestry is modelled with a proxy; the Luxmanda result could reflect migration from the Levant or a shared earlier ancestral population. The authors' hypothesis involves an unsampled northeastern African group. Mixing with foragers continued, so the group is not uniform across sites or time.

populations.name: Iron Age farmers with western-African-related ancestry
populations.description: Iron Age individuals in eastern and southern Africa whose ancestry is mostly related to present-day western African populations. They are associated with the spread of farming, which in some regions brought near-complete replacement of local forager ancestry and elsewhere involved mixing.
caveats: A linguistic label (Bantu) is used here only to describe an association; the population is defined genetically.

overview.heading: Who they were
overview.text: This group holds Iron Age individuals in eastern and southern Africa whose ancestry is mostly related to present-day western African and Bantu-speaking populations. It is defined by ancestry and by association with the spread of farming, not by language. Examples include a 600-year-old person from the Zanzibar archipelago, an Iron Age child at Deloraine Farm in Kenya, and Late Iron Age people of Zambia and South Africa.

overview.heading: Ancestry
overview.text: Their ancestry is related to present-day western Africans, with extra components. A 600-year-old individual from the Zanzibar archipelago has even more western African-related ancestry than present-day Bantu speakers in Kenya, who themselves mix western and eastern African-related ancestry dated to 800-400 years ago. In Botswana, individuals carry mostly Bantu-related ancestry with 10-40% southern African hunter-gatherer ancestry.

overview.heading: What came before and after
overview.text: The spread of farmers from western Africa nearly completely replaced local hunter-gatherers in some regions, such as Malawi, where little earlier ancestry is detected. Elsewhere it involved mixing: Bantu-speaking populations received significant gene flow from local groups.
