Eastern hunter-gatherer (Sidelkino-cluster) ancestry is a mixture of Villabruna/Oberkassel and ancient north Eurasian ancestry, dated by admixture analysis to about 15,000-13,000 years ago in old Sidelkino-cluster individuals (Peschanitsa 13,000 years ago, Minino 11,000 years ago), which also show extra Oberkassel affinity, possibly because the mix varied while the profile was forming.
evidence.location: Results, Post-14 ka to Neolithic; Extended Data Fig. 7

evidence.claim: The Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov group from Karelia (about 8,200 years ago, 19 genomes) is indistinguishable from the oldest Sidelkino-cluster individual, 11,000-year-old Sidelkino from Samara; Sidelkino-cluster individuals show higher frequencies of mitochondrial haplogroups U2, U4 and R1b and uniquely Y haplogroups Q, R and J.
evidence.location: Results, Post-14 ka to Neolithic; Extended Data Figs. 1-2

evidence.claim: Oberkassel-related ancestry appears in eastern European hunter-gatherers by about 7,500 years ago at Minino I and Yazykovo in the upper Volga region, though reservoir effects may make radiocarbon dates there up to about 500 years too old.

Satsurblia (13,132-13,380 years ago, 1.4x coverage) and Kotias Klde (9,529-9,895 years ago, 15.4x coverage) are two males from western Georgia who form a clade excluding other pre-Bronze Age genomes, showing continuity between the Late Upper Palaeolithic and the Mesolithic there.

Present-day southern Caucasus populations are the closest to Caucasus hunter-gatherers, suggesting regional continuity of about 13,000 years; CHG and early farmers form a clade relative to western hunter-gatherers, and CHG show a high frequency of long runs of homozygosity, indicating a small population.
evidence.note: Part of this inference rests on present-day genomes.

evidence.claim: Model-based splits (G-PhoCS) place the separation of western hunter-gatherers from the ancestors of Caucasus hunter-gatherers and farmers at about 40-50,000 years ago, and CHG from early farmers at about 25,000 years ago.
evidence.note: Estimates depend on the genomes used and the assumed mutation rate.

evidence.claim: The Satsurblia-cluster Caucasus hunter-gatherers (13,000-10,000 years ago) are related to the population that contributed new alleles to the Villabruna cluster, but cannot be the direct source because they carry large Basal Eurasian ancestry while Villabruna-cluster individuals do not.
evidence.location: Results, A drawing together of the ancestry of Europe and the Near East

evidence.claim: Seven Iberomaurusian-associated individuals about 15,000 years old from Taforalt, Morocco were studied; they have genetic affinity with early Holocene Near Easterners, best represented by Natufians, show no evidence of gene flow from Palaeolithic Europeans, and carry about one third sub-Saharan African-related ancestry.
evidence.note: Abstract only; full text not open access.

evidence.claim: The sub-Saharan African-related ancestry in the Taforalt individuals is best approximated by a mixture of components found in present-day West and East Africans, and the study reports that the individuals link Near Eastern and sub-Saharan African populations.
evidence.note: Abstract only; proxies from present-day genomes.

evidence.claim: The Natufian-associated sample comes from Raqefet Cave in the Levant (12,000-9,800 BCE); Natufians derive about 44% (plus or minus 8) of their ancestry from a Basal Eurasian lineage, similar to the earliest Iranian samples, so they are not shown to be the vector that brought it into the Near East.
evidence.location: Results, Basal Eurasian ancestry was pervasive in the ancient Near East
evidence.note: qpAdm estimate; Basal Eurasian is a modelled lineage.

evidence.claim: Natufians and successor Levantine Neolithic populations carried Y haplogroup E, of likely African origin, but no genome-wide affinity of Natufians to sub-Saharan Africans is evident; Levantine early farmers share significantly more alleles with Natufians than with Iranian early farmers.

Using the Ethiopian Mota genome as an African reference, Basal Eurasian ancestry is estimated at 38.5% (plus or minus 5.0) in Natufians and 24.8% (plus or minus 5.5) in the Pinarbasi Anatolian hunter-gatherer, a lower estimate than the first study's 44% for Natufians.
evidence.note: Different method and proxy from Lazaridis 2016.

evidence.claim: The first Epipaleolithic Anatolian hunter-gatherer genome (AHG) comes from Pinarbasi, directly dated to 13,642-13,073 cal BCE; in PCA it is intermediate between western hunter-gatherers and Epipaleolithic/Neolithic Levantines, and distinct from both.

Early aceramic Anatolian farmers (about 8300-7800 BCE, Boncuklu) derive most of their ancestry (89.7%, plus or minus 3.9) from an AHG-related population with the rest Iranian/Caucasus-related; later ceramic-period farmers still derive 78.7% (plus or minus 3.5) from the earlier farmers, with additional Levant Neolithic-related ancestry.
evidence.note: qpAdm models.

evidence.claim: Iron Gates Mesolithic hunter-gatherers from the Balkans show the highest genetic affinity to the Pinarbasi hunter-gatherer and the second highest to Natufians; the authors read this as evidence of a genetic link between southern Europe and the Near East older than 15,000 years, with Near Eastern gene flow into the ancestors of Iron Gates hunter-gatherers.

Early European Farmers (Stuttgart) are modelled in an admixture graph as deriving 44% (plus or minus 10) of their ancestry from a 'Basal Eurasian' lineage that split before the divergence of other non-African lineages; no sampled individual belongs to it.
evidence.note: Modelled ghost lineage.

evidence.claim: Basal Eurasian ancestry estimates are highest in the earliest Iranian and Levantine populations: 66% (plus or minus 13) in a likely Mesolithic Iranian, 48% (plus or minus 6) in Iranian Neolithic and 44% (plus or minus 8) in Natufians; by extrapolation the lineage had little if any Neanderthal ancestry (95% interval 0-60%).
evidence.location: Results, Basal Eurasian ancestry was pervasive in the ancient Near East; Fig. 2

evidence.claim: The authors give two possible explanations for the high Basal Eurasian share in Near Eastern groups: thorough mixing into the Near East after the main Neanderthal admixture, or ancestors who always lived in the Near East in a lineage that did not take part in that admixture.
An alternative estimate for Basal Eurasian ancestry, using the ancient Ethiopian Mota genome as a proxy, gives 38.5% in Natufians and 24.8% in a 15,000-year-old Anatolian hunter-gatherer.

Tests find no support for an earlier model that European pre-Neolithic individuals such as Kostenki 14 carried Basal Eurasian ancestry; the Villabruna-cluster Europeans of the time do not have it, while the Caucasus hunter-gatherers do.
evidence.location: Results, A single founding population; A drawing together of the ancestry

evidence.claim: Four Early Neolithic genomes from Iran were sequenced: Wezmeh Cave (WC1, 7,455-7,082 cal BCE, 10x coverage) and three roughly 10,000-year-old individuals from Tepe Abdul Hosein (0.6-1.2x); diet isotopes in WC1 indicate a diet rich in cultivated C3 cereals.

Early farmers from Ganj Dareh in the Zagros (8,200-7,600 BCE) share alleles at an equal rate with Anatolian and Levantine early farmers, which the authors read as long-term isolation of western Iran; Iranian Neolithic samples have about 48% Basal Eurasian ancestry.

A population related to Chalcolithic-period individuals from western Iran is modelled as contributing about 43% of the ancestry of Early Bronze Age steppe populations, about 44% of Levantine Bronze Age ancestry and about 33% of Chalcolithic northwestern Anatolians; the Chalcolithic Iranians themselves are modelled as a mix of Zagros Neolithic, Levant and Caucasus hunter-gatherer ancestry.
evidence.location: Results, How diverse first farmers mixed; The Near Eastern contribution

evidence.claim: The Zagros genomes show a large effective ancestral population (lowest short ROH of the ancient genomes tested) and share more than 95% of recent ancestry with modern groups from the Middle East, Caucasus and India.
evidence.note: Part rests on present-day genomes.

evidence.claim: Pre-Pottery Neolithic farmers from 'Ain Ghazal and Motza in the southern Levant (8,300-6,700 BCE) trace about two thirds of their ancestry to people related to Natufian hunter-gatherers and about one third to people related to Anatolian farmers.
evidence.location: Results, How diverse first farmers mixed
evidence.note: qpAdm.

evidence.claim: Two Levantine Pre-Pottery Neolithic B farmers (Kfar HaHoresh, about 7700-7600 BCE; Ba'ja, 7027-6685 cal BCE) were added and used as Levant Neolithic references.

East African ancestry related to the Near East is significantly better modelled by Levantine early farmers than by Anatolian or early European farmers; the authors take this to mean it did not spread from the group that carried Near Eastern ancestry into Europe.
evidence.note: Skoglund 2017 notes this could instead be a shared earlier ancestral population.

evidence.claim: Early farmers of mainland Europe descend from a population related to Neolithic northwestern Anatolians (European farmers share more alleles with Anatolian Neolithic than with Levantine Neolithic farmers, Z=15), but the authors note that the spatial distribution of Anatolian-like farmer populations is unknown, so other sources are not rejected.
evidence.location: Results, The Near Eastern contribution to Europeans

evidence.claim: Neolithic populations of Bulgaria, Croatia, Macedonia, Serbia and Romania cluster closely with northwestern Anatolian Neolithic farmers; modelled as Anatolian Neolithic plus western hunter-gatherer, about 98% (95% CI 97-100%) of Balkan Neolithic ancestry is Anatolian-related.
evidence.location: Results, Population transformations in the first farmers

evidence.claim: The Anatolian/European farmer lineage is modelled as separating from European hunter-gatherers about 33-39,000 years ago and from the Neolithic Zagros lineage about 46-77,000 years ago.

Twenty-two individuals from Peqi'in Cave were analysed, of whom 20 appear unrelated; nine of ten males carry Y haplogroup T, unlike earlier Levantine populations dominated by E and later Bronze Age individuals all of J.

The Peqi'in population cannot be the sole ancestor of all later Bronze Age groups: one Bronze Age group could not plausibly have descended from the same population as Peqi'in, and several three-way models with similar sources fit the data (Anatolia Neolithic and early European farmers are hard to distinguish).

Eight of nine individuals from Malak Preslavets (Bulgaria, mid-6th millennium BCE) carry more hunter-gatherer ancestry than other Balkan farmers, modelled as 82% Anatolian Neolithic-related, 15% western hunter-gatherer-related and 4% eastern hunter-gatherer-related.

At Lepenski Vir in the Iron Gates, two individuals dated 6200-5600 BCE have entirely Anatolian Neolithic-related ancestry and isotope data indicate they were migrants; the Iron Gates were a region of interaction between groups distinct in ancestry and subsistence.

One early Starcevo individual from Hungary has 7.8% (plus or minus 1.7) hunter-gatherer ancestry with a very recent admixture date, while most early Neolithic Hungarian samples do not differ significantly from Neolithic Anatolians; hunter-gatherer ancestry rose gradually through the Neolithic.

Balkan Copper Age populations harbor significantly more hunter-gatherer-related ancestry than Balkan Neolithic populations (Z=4.3), roughly contemporary with the hunter-gatherer 'resurgence' reported in central Europe and Iberia.

Five southern Greek Neolithic individuals (Peloponnese, about 4000 BCE) and one Bulgarian Neolithic individual are shifted toward Caucasus hunter-gatherers and away from western hunter-gatherers relative to other Anatolian and Balkan Neolithic individuals.

LBK farmers (Germany) have about 4-5% hunter-gatherer ancestry with an average admixture date of 5545 BCE (plus or minus 65), the hunter-gatherer source being most closely related to a combination of two Mesolithic genomes though not statistically significantly; the analysis pooled Stuttgart with LBK samples from farther northeast such as Halberstadt.
evidence.location: Results, Germany transect; Extended Data Table 3

evidence.claim: At the Blatterhohle site in Germany, three Middle Neolithic individuals classed as farmers by isotopes carried 40-50% hunter-gatherer ancestry, at a site where farmer and hunter-gatherer occupation overlapped late; the German Middle Neolithic grouping overall has about 17%.
Hunter-gatherer admixture in farmers of the north and west was male-biased in later periods, unlike the groups that stayed in southeastern Europe, which mixed extensively without male bias.

In Iberia, the average hunter-gatherer admixture date for the Early Neolithic is 5650 BCE (plus or minus 65), rising to 5860 BCE when only the five oldest samples are used; with farming thought to begin in Spain around 5500 BCE this suggests some hunter-gatherer ancestry was acquired along the migration route.
Strong genetic substructure existed between northwestern and southeastern Iberian hunter-gatherers before farming spread, and the study analyses 44 new Neolithic individuals from the peninsula.

Haplotype-based analyses show British Neolithic genomes are more similar to Irish and Iberian Neolithic genomes than to central European ones, consistent with the same ancestral populations bringing farming along the Mediterranean route to Britain and Ireland.

The study analysed six Mesolithic and 67 Neolithic individuals from Britain (8500-2500 BCE; earliest Neolithic 3951-3780 cal BCE at McArthur Cave, Scotland); all British Mesolithic individuals cluster with western hunter-gatherers.

Neolithic WHG admixture is geographically structured: Wales has the lowest, followed by south-west and central England, with higher values in south-east England and Scotland, and the elevated levels in south-east England are older, probably acquired on the continent; only Raschoille Cave individuals show introgression within about 10 generations.

The authors conclude that the appearance of Neolithic practices in Britain around 4000 BCE was mediated overwhelmingly by immigration of farmers from continental Europe, strongly rejecting adoption by indigenous hunter-gatherers as the main process, and found only low levels of local hunter-gatherer introgression.

Eleven outliers are identified, 3 at Gonur (2500-2000 BCE, Turkmenistan) and 8 at Shahr-i-Sokhta (3300-2000 BCE, eastern Iran), with 11-50% ancestry related to Andamanese hunter-gatherers and the rest from a mixture of Iranian farmer- and West Siberian hunter-gatherer-related ancestry (about 50-89%), and no detectable Anatolian farmer-related ancestry.
evidence.location: Results, An Ancestry Profile Widespread During the Indus Valley Civilization

evidence.claim: The authors state they cannot be definitive that this cline, the Indus Periphery Cline, was also common in the Indus Valley Civilization without ancient DNA from IVC contexts, and offer six circumstantial lines of evidence; the mixture that formed the cline is dated to about 5400-3700 BCE, a millennium or more before the mature IVC.

Sixty-one skeletal samples from the Rakhigarhi cemetery of the Indus Valley Civilization (mature IVC dated 2600-1900 BCE) were tried and only one, I6113, yielded enough authentic DNA; it projects onto the Indus Periphery Cline, which is significantly depleted in steppe pastoralist-related ancestry (p=0.018) relative to the later South Asian mixture.
evidence.note: One genome.

evidence.claim: The Iranian-related ancestry in the IVC Cline derives from a lineage that diverged before the ancestors of early Iranian hunter-gatherers, herders and farmers separated, so sampled genomes from the Iranian plateau and the IVC descend from different hunter-gatherer groups who began farming without being linked by movement of people.
evidence.note: Contradicts the earlier proposal of eastward spread of Iranian farmers.

evidence.claim: The Indus Periphery Cline contributes the majority of the ancestry of present-day South Asians; Ancestral South Indians are estimated at a minimum of 55% Indus Periphery-related (with the most Iranian-farmer-related individual as source) and the remainder Andamanese hunter-gatherer-related, and the Steppe Cline has one end on the Indus Periphery Cline and the other about 41% Central Steppe MLBA and 59% an Iranian-rich Indus Periphery subgroup.
evidence.location: Results, Three Ancestry Clines; The ASI and ANI arose

evidence.claim: AASI is fitted in an admixture graph with Palliyar and Juang as an Asian lineage that split off around the time East Asian, Andaman Islander and Australian ancestors separated; Juang can only be fitted with extra AASI ancestry beyond ASI, so groups with less Iranian farmer-related ancestry than ASI also existed.
evidence.note: Uses present-day groups; no unmixed AASI individual is sampled.

evidence.claim: Several tribal groups of southern India are consistent with about 0% Central Steppe MLBA ancestry and the most extreme position for the Ancestral South Indians, which the authors model as at least 55% Indus Periphery-related and the remainder Andamanese hunter-gatherer-related, a stand-in for AASI.
evidence.location: Results, The ASI and ANI Arose

evidence.claim: Using admixture dating on the southern Indian Palliyar group, the mixing of Iranian farmer-related and AASI-related ancestry is dated 107 plus or minus 11 generations ago, a 95% interval of 1700-400 BCE at 28 years per generation, so the ASI were not fully formed at the time of the IVC.
evidence.location: Results, The ASI and ANI Arose; Discussion
evidence.note: DATES from a present-day population.

evidence.claim: Neither the ASI nor ANI is directly sampled; the authors co-analyse ancient and present-day groups to reconstruct them, and note that the ASI formed after 2000 BCE as a mixture of a point on the Indus Periphery Cline with South Asians holding more AASI ancestry; ASI and ANI then mixed to form the Modern Indian Cline.

Steppe-related ancestry in the Swat Valley time series (117 individuals, 1400 BCE-1700 CE) is dated to about 1900-1500 BCE (26 generations before they lived), and the Kalash's admixture is dated 110 plus or minus 12 generations ago; the Steppe Cline runs from a point on the Indus Periphery Cline to a mix of about 41% Central Steppe MLBA and 59% an Iranian-rich Indus Periphery subgroup.
evidence.location: Results, The Steppe Cline; The ASI and ANI Arose

evidence.claim: In Late Bronze Age and Iron Age Swat individuals, steppe-related ancestry is 5% of Y chromosomes against 20% of autosomes, so it entered largely through females there, whereas in present-day South Asians there is an excess on the Y chromosome, so sex bias varied by place and time.
evidence.location: Results, Steppe Ancestry is Primarily from Males
evidence.note: Mixed sex-bias evidence.

evidence.claim: Outliers in Turan dated about 2100-1500 BCE carry steppe pastoralist-derived ancestry in mixed form, and later steppe-derived groups such as Scythians, Sarmatians, Kushans and Huns cannot be major sources of South Asia's steppe ancestry because they carry too much East Asian-related ancestry.

Papuan and Aboriginal Australian ancestors diversified 25-40 thousand years ago, all Aboriginal Australians descend from a single founding population differentiated about 10-32 thousand years ago, and Aboriginal Australians and Papuans diverged from Eurasians 51-72 thousand years ago after a single dispersal out of Africa (when archaic admixture is taken into account).
evidence.note: Model-based estimates from present-day genomes.

evidence.claim: The number of putative Denisovan haplotypes correlates almost perfectly (r squared 0.96) with Australo-Papuan ancestry per individual, and a Denisovan pulse is estimated at 31-50 thousand years ago in a site frequency spectrum model.
evidence.location: Results, Archaic admixture; Extended Data Fig. 3

evidence.claim: A model of two out-of-Africa waves, with Australo-Papuan ancestors dispersing about 14 thousand years before Eurasians, fits when only modern humans are modelled, but when archaic Neanderthal and Denisovan admixture is included a single out-of-Africa bottleneck about 72 thousand years ago (95% CI 60-104) is supported.

The study sequenced three individuals from Teouma, Efate (Vanuatu), radiocarbon dated 3110-2740 BP and Lapita-period, and one individual from Talasiu, Tonga (2680-2340 BP); all four were female; they cluster tightly with each other and, like Taiwanese Ami and Atayal, are not shifted toward Papuan ancestry as present-day Remote Oceanians are.

The ancient individuals and the Taiwanese Ami are consistent with descending from a common ancestral population, and the best-fitting qpGraph model has present-day Polynesians as mixtures of First Remote Oceanians and a Papuan population related to Highland New Guineans.

The study compared Vanuatu and Tonga individuals dated 2900-2600 years ago with 14 ancient Vanuatu individuals and 185 present-day people from 18 islands; a dramatic turnover in Vanuatu is apparent after about 2900 and before about 2300 years ago.

Nineteen individuals from Vanuatu, Tonga, French Polynesia and the Solomon Islands (about 2,600-200 years ago) show Papuan-related ancestry arriving from about 2,500 years ago: the earliest post-Lapita individual (TAN002) has no Austronesian ancestry, Malakula individuals over about 500 years from 2,500 BP carry 22-46% Austronesian ancestry, and 1,100-year-old Futuna individuals 11-17%.

Excess Austronesian X-chromosome ancestry in the Malakula time series shows sex-biased admixture in progress (one male with a Papuan Y lineage carries about 50% Austronesian maternal excess), and the latest individual (TAN001) is modelled as descended directly from a Baining-related population, suggesting complete local replacement.

Papuan ancestry in the 14 ancient Vanuatu individuals is nearly total in early post-Lapita individuals and later diluted; an ancient pair about 1,300 years old gives an admixture date of 18 plus or minus 6 generations (about 500 years) earlier, which falls in the range of admixture dates for present-day groups.

Present-day Vanuatu could not be fitted alongside the ancient individuals in one model, indicating that present-day ni-Vanuatu may carry an additional genetic component not found in the ancient samples; the two studies differ in emphasis between one large movement and incremental, repeated, sex-biased admixture.

The arrival of almost entirely Papuan-ancestry people in Vanuatu likely reflects migrations a few hundred years before 2,300 years ago, at the end of the Lapita period, when there is also evidence of changes in skeletal morphology and the end of long-distance trade between Near and Remote Oceania.

A fine-grained analysis of ancestry profiles shows the Papuan ancestry in Vanuatu derives from the Bismarck Archipelago rather than the geographically closer Solomon Islands, while the Papuan ancestry in Polynesia derives from different sources, a third stream of migration from Near to Remote Oceania.

Baining groups of New Britain are the closest present-day proxy sources for the Near Oceanian ancestry in the earliest post-Lapita Vanuatu individual, whose affinity is not explained by shared Austronesian ancestry; a qpGraph model derives the individual from a population ancestral to Baining Marabu.
evidence.note: Present-day proxies stand in for an unsampled ancient source.

evidence.claim: The authors describe Cucuteni-Trypillia farming groups as spreading east across the Carpathians to the Dnipro Valley around 4800 BCE, with ancestry mainly derived from early European farmers plus some western hunter-gatherer ancestry (summarising earlier work).
evidence.note: Background statement drawing on earlier studies, not a new result.

evidence.claim: For 23 of 24 sampled Trypillia individuals a three-source model fits, averaging about 81% Balkan Eneolithic (farmer-related), 14% Balkan hunter-gatherer-related and 5% Caucasus-Lower Volga-derived ancestry; mixing is dated to 4595 BCE, 95% interval 4832-4358 BCE.
evidence.location: Results, Trypillia and Usatove; Table 1; Fig. 3
evidence.note: qpAdm and DATES estimates; depend on the proxy source groups chosen.

evidence.claim: Usatove-associated people are modelled as about 45% from an intermediate Caucasus-Lower Volga-cline group and about 55% Trypillia-associated farmers, with the mixing dated to 4471 BCE (95% interval 4571-4371 BCE); the CLV share in Trypillia itself is only about 5%.
evidence.location: Results, Trypillia and Usatove; Discussion; Table 1

evidence.claim: The authors offer several untested settings for the Usatove mixing: a trading outpost in the Danube-Dniester delta, a coexisting 'commonwealth' of cultures, or Trypillia farmers under dominance by CLV-related groups; the DNA does not choose between them.

Globular Amphora (GAC) individuals from Bohemia carry the most hunter-gatherer-related ancestry (25.7%, plus or minus 1.4) among the pre-Corded Ware groups there, and the admixture dates suggest GAC reflects a nonlocal arrival from a region with more hunter-gatherer gene flow, such as Poland.
evidence.location: Results, Bohemia before Corded Ware; Fig. 3B
evidence.note: qpAdm and DATES; Bohemian GAC only.

evidence.claim: Sixteen Rivnac and GAC individuals who lived at or after the time Corded Ware appeared in Bohemia show no detectable steppe ancestry, suggesting little biological exchange from Corded Ware/Yamnaya-related people into these groups.

The farmer-related ancestry in Corded Ware-associated individuals can be modelled as coming exclusively from a Globular Amphora-associated genetic cluster, and it co-occurs with steppe-related ancestry across all sampled European regions; the authors infer that steppe-related ancestry spread mostly through groups already mixed with GAC-related farmers.
evidence.note: Supervised ancestry modelling with proxy sources.

evidence.claim: Before Corded Ware appeared, eastern GAC and western Yamnaya groups exchanged cultural elements in the forest-steppe zone northwest of the Black Sea; the authors treat such contact zones as probably central to Corded Ware formation, but note that earlier data from few individuals had suggested only cultural influence.

Using Globular Amphora as a stand-in for farmer-related ancestry, Yamnaya from Samara carry about 13% and Yamnaya from Ukraine or the Caucasus about 17% such ancestry, with the authors noting the source was a mixture of farmer ancestry and at least 20% western hunter-gatherer ancestry.
evidence.location: Results, Yamnaya and steppe groups; Fig. 4; Supplementary Table 17
evidence.note: Globular Amphora is used as a proximate surrogate, not as a proven source.

evidence.claim: Two Yamna outlier individuals from Moldova with substantial European-farmer ancestry are best fitted as Core Yamna plus either Trypillia or Globular Amphora ancestry.
evidence.location: Results, Yamna ancestry and Caucasus admixture
evidence.note: Model with several fitting alternatives.

evidence.claim: Burials at Ekaterinovka (5050-4450 BCE) already carry about 24% ancestry related to the Lower Volga Berezhnovka group, while an earlier hunter-gatherer from Lebyazhinka carries a share consistent with zero (7.9% plus or minus 3.6).
evidence.note: qpAdm; Ekaterinovka dates from herbivore bone radiocarbon dates.

evidence.claim: At Khvalynsk (4500-4350 BCE) individuals form a gradient with about 77% (high), 57% (medium) and 41% (low) Berezhnovka-related ancestry; across the Volga cline the Berezhnovka-related share ranges roughly 14-89%.
evidence.note: Two-source qpAdm model with Karelia hunter-gatherers as the other source.

evidence.claim: A Volga-cline individual from Csongrad in Hungary (4331-4073 BCE) has about 88% Berezhnovka-related ancestry, comparable to the highest Khvalynsk individuals, which the authors read as long-distance contact that skipped the Dnipro and Don basins.

The origin of Lower Volga (Berezhnovka) ancestry is unresolved: there are no earlier sequenced individuals from the Lower Volga, the CHG-related source is unsampled, and the group cannot be modelled as continuous with contemporaneous or earlier groups.
The upriver Eastern hunter-gatherer ancestry of the Volga cline has long-established eastern European antecedents, whereas the downriver Berezhnovka-related ancestry does not.
Yamnaya individuals cannot be traced to the Volga cline: Core Yamnaya fit neither the Volga cline nor the CLV cline directly and are placed on the Dnipro cline instead.

The Caucasus-Lower Volga cline runs from the Neolithic Caucasus (Aknashen) through Maikop and Remontnoye to Berezhnovka on the Lower Volga; the main Maikop cluster is modelled as about 86% Aknashen-related and the Remontnoye group as about 45% Aknashen-related plus Berezhnovka-related ancestry.
Berezhnovka-2 individuals (4450-3960 BCE) on the Lower Volga carry about 29% Central Asian (Siberian-related) ancestry in one model, which the Lower Don Krivyansky group lacks (about 5%).

Berezhnovka-related ancestry makes up about 27% of Chalcolithic Armenians at Areni-1 (around 4000 BCE) and about 11% (with a Berezhnovka-related source) or 19% (with a Remontnoye-related source) of Bronze Age central Anatolians; the exact steppe-related source in Anatolia cannot be fixed.
evidence.location: Results, CLV impact in Armenia and Anatolia
evidence.note: Authors say the source is not precisely determined.

evidence.claim: Some carriers of Volga-CLV ancestry, as at Giurgiulesti and Csongrad, advanced to the Balkans and Carpathian region largely without mixing with people on the way, while Trypillia and Usatove incorporated CLV ancestry in different amounts (about 5% and about 50%).

Serednii Stih is represented by 13 individuals (4996-3372 BCE, radiocarbon dates uncorrected for freshwater reservoir effects) who are spread along the Dnipro cline, in contrast to the genetically homogeneous Core Yamnaya.
evidence.note: Dates may be inflated where freshwater fish were eaten.

evidence.claim: The Dnipro cline is fitted as Caucasus-Lower Volga-related ancestry mixed with a Dnipro/Don hunter-gatherer source: Yamnaya are inferred to have about a fifth of their ancestry from that source (22.5% from a Middle Don individual, or 17.7% from Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherers).

Serednii Stih people lacked appreciable European-farmer ancestry, unlike Usatove; the authors read Core Yamna as a late Serednii Stih-derived population with more CLV ancestry than sampled Stih individuals but the same components.

All Dnipro-cline groups, Serednii Stih included, can be well modelled as a mixture of Ukraine Neolithic or Middle Don hunter-gatherers at one extreme and Core Yamnaya at the other; the hunter-gatherer source is from the Dnipro-Don area, not the Volga.

Knowledge of steppe populations like Serednii Stih has been limited by small samples with highly variable ancestry, and the authors note that data on the Epipaleolithic to Early Bronze Age North Pontic region come from limited sites.

The Maikop culture is known for large, rich burial mounds. Twelve individuals from eight sites in the northern Caucasus foothills (Maikop, Novosvobodnaya at Klady, Late Maikop) appear genetically homogeneous and resemble the preceding Eneolithic Caucasus individuals, a continuation of the local profile that persists until about 1100 BCE in later Caucasus groups.
evidence.location: Results, Genetic ancestry in the Caucasus

evidence.claim: Caucasus groups, including Maikop, are modelled as 40-72% Anatolian Chalcolithic-related and 28-60% Caucasus hunter-gatherer-related ancestry; using southeastern European farmer sources instead shifts the hunter-gatherer share to 51-70%, and unsampled populations could fit as well.
evidence.note: Proxy-dependent range.

evidence.claim: The main Maikop cluster (kurgan burials at Klady and Dlinnaya-Polyana, 3932-2934 BCE for Maikop overall) is modelled as about 86% Aknashen (Neolithic Armenia)-related ancestry, with Lower Volga ancestry about one seventh of the total; Maikop burials were contracted on one side, unlike the steppe pose.

Steppe Maykop individuals from grass-steppe mounds lack the Anatolian farmer-related component and carry extra ancient North Eurasian and Native American-related ancestry, so they differ from foothill Maikop individuals.
evidence.location: Results, Ancient North Eurasian ancestry in Steppe Maykop individuals

evidence.claim: Core Yamnaya (104 high-quality individuals) are genetically homogeneous across a sampling range of about 5,000 km from Hungary to southern Siberia (mean FST 0.005), and the mixing that formed their ancestry is dated to 4038 BCE (plus or minus 48 years).
evidence.note: Dating by an admixture-tract method; the mixture may have begun earlier or continued later.

evidence.claim: Identical-by-descent segment sharing shows Yamnaya individuals in a kurgan were mostly unrelated: about 14% of pairs within kurgans and 7% across kurgans of the same cemetery were close relatives, so kurgans were not mainly family tombs.

Core Yamnaya Y chromosomes are almost all R-M269 (49 of 51), mostly sub-lineage R-Z2103 (41 of 51), while the Don Yamnaya are dominated by I-L699 (17 of 20), showing continuity with local hunter-gatherer ancestors.

Many Yamnaya in south-eastern Europe cluster with Core Yamnaya, but others deviate toward Neolithic and Chalcolithic groups of south-eastern and central Europe, with that mixing in the late 4th millennium BCE; the Don Yamnaya (about 79% Core Yamnaya, 21% Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherer) expanded little.
evidence.location: Results, The Yamnaya expansion; Extended Data Fig. 3

evidence.claim: The Core Yamnaya fit the Dnipro cline, which suggests a Dnipro basin origin, but an origin in the Don area cannot be excluded, and Core Yamnaya used as a source for earlier populations must stand in for an unsampled Eneolithic source.

Steppe-related ancestry (Steppe_5000BP_4300BP) is modelled as about 65% Middle Don hunter-gatherer-related and about 35% Caucasus hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, which the authors present as a previously unknown proximal source.
evidence.location: Results; Extended Data Fig. 6; Supplementary Data 9
evidence.note: A competing model of Yamnaya formation (see disagreements).

evidence.claim: Because Y-chromosome haplogroups differ between Corded Ware and Yamnaya, published Yamnaya genomes may not be the most direct source of steppe ancestry in early Corded Ware groups; denser sampling across the steppe horizon is needed to find that source.

Catacomb-complex individuals, which partly overlap and follow Yamna in the North Pontic region, are consistent with Core Yamna ancestry, so Yamna genetic ancestry persisted there into the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE.
evidence.location: Results, Yamna ancestry in the Bronze Age

evidence.claim: The earliest Corded Ware individuals in Bohemia date to about 3010-2889 BCE, and Corded Ware was widespread there by 2900 BCE; early Corded Ware individuals are genetically very diverse, including four females with no steppe ancestry.

Models combining any single Yamnaya source with a central European Neolithic source fit early Bohemian Corded Ware poorly; adding about 5-15% of Latvia Middle Neolithic/Ukraine Neolithic/Pitted Ware-like ancestry improves fits.

Y-chromosome diversity fell from five lineages in early Corded Ware to one dominant lineage (R1a-M417) in late Corded Ware in Bohemia, which cannot be explained by chance and implies a process affecting males more than autosomal diversity.
The authors interpret early Corded Ware in Bohemia as a plural society that joined people of different ancestries and histories, with female-biased assimilation of people lacking steppe ancestry.
evidence.note: Interpretation by the authors from a Bohemian transect.

evidence.claim: The study analysed 133 Beaker-associated individuals from central Europe, and outside Iberia most Beaker-associated males carry Y-haplogroup R1b-M269 (84 of 90).

Outside Iberia, the Neolithic-related ancestry in Beaker-associated individuals is most closely related to central and northern European Neolithic groups, whereas in Iberian Beaker-associated individuals it fits local Iberian Middle Neolithic and Copper Age groups best.

In Bohemia, 56 late Bell Beaker individuals (2400 BCE or later) carry about 20% more local Middle Eneolithic-like ancestry than 3 early Bell Beaker individuals, who resemble Corded Ware and are all female.
evidence.note: The early sample is only three individuals.

evidence.claim: At the start of the Early Bronze Age in Bohemia, ancestry changed again: the pre-classical Unetice group is modelled as 63.5% early Beaker-related and 36.5% late Beaker-related ancestry, or in an alternative model as an estimated 47.7% replacement involving a north-eastern source.
evidence.note: Two models with different results; authors stress limited resolution.

evidence.claim: Bell Beaker males mostly carry Y lineage R1b-P312, which has not been found among Corded Ware or Yamnaya males, so these three groups cannot currently be linked as paternal sources of one another despite sharing steppe ancestry.

British Beaker-associated individuals (37) closely resemble central European Beaker individuals; Oostwoud (Netherlands) individuals are most closely related to southern British Beaker individuals, though not necessarily direct ancestors of them.
evidence.location: Results, Nearly complete turnover of ancestry in Britain

evidence.claim: Between about 2450 and 2000 BCE ancestry proportions in Britain varied, consistent with migrant communities beginning to mix with the Neolithic population (51 Neolithic individuals studied, none with steppe affinity); after 2000 BCE individuals were more uniform.
evidence.location: Results, Nearly complete turnover of ancestry in Britain; Fig. 3

evidence.claim: Earlier work described Neolithic Britain as about 80% early-European-farmer and 20% western hunter-gatherer ancestry, stable for roughly a millennium and a half until about 2450 BCE, when migration with Beaker traditions brought a third, steppe-related, ancestry component (minimum 90% from new migrants).
evidence.note: Summary of earlier studies, including Olalde 2018.

evidence.claim: In Iberian Beaker-associated individuals the best-fitting source of Neolithic-related ancestry was local Middle Neolithic and Copper Age populations, excluding central and northern European sources (P < 0.0063); their Y haplogroups included I (5) and G2 (1), common in earlier Neolithic Europe.
Four Iberian Beaker-associated individuals with a steppe genome-wide signal carry Y haplogroup R1b-M269, the lineage common among Beaker males elsewhere.

The Copper Age dataset includes 47 new individuals; one male from Camino de las Yeseras (2473-2030 cal BCE) clusters with North Africans, an example of sporadic Copper Age contact with North Africa that had limited impact.

The earliest steppe-related ancestry in the Bronze Age is in 14 Iberians dated about 2500-2000 BCE who lived alongside local people without it; after 2000 BCE the groups admixed, giving about 40% ancestry from incoming groups.

Y-chromosome turnover in Bronze Age Iberia was more dramatic than for the genome overall: lineages common in the Copper Age (I2, G2, H) were nearly replaced by R1b-M269, and non-local ancestry was lower on the X chromosome, which points to more incoming males than females.
The Bronze Age dataset grew from 7 to 60 individuals (about 2200-900 BCE); steppe-related ancestry appeared throughout Iberia, but with less impact in the south.

In the Iron Age, ancestry related to north and central Europe rose relative to the Bronze Age by 10-19% (15 eastern coastal individuals), 11-31% (2 in the southwest) and 28-43% (3 in the north), suggesting gene flow in the Late Bronze or early Iron Age.

EEF-related ancestry in England and Wales rose from 31.0% (n=69, Copper Age/Early Bronze Age) to 34.7% (Middle Bronze Age, n=26), 36.1% (Late Bronze Age, n=23) and 37.9% (Iron Age, n=273), with no significant change in Scotland.

The study generated genome-wide data from 793 individuals, increasing Middle to Late Bronze and Iron Age data from Britain 12-fold, and noted that Welsh sample sizes are too small for accurate inference.
evidence.note: Covers all of Britain and neighbouring regions.

evidence.claim: The steppe-related ancestry that reached Central and South Asia came from a secondary expansion of a group with about 67% Yamnaya-related (Western_Steppe_EMBA) and about 33% ancestry from the European Cline (a gradient formed by farmers from Anatolia mixing with European hunter-gatherers), a group that included Corded Ware, Srubnaya, Petrovka and Sintashta complexes.
evidence.note: Modelled; authors say they replicate earlier findings.

evidence.claim: Fifty individuals from the Sintashta cemetery of Kamennyi Ambar V include several sets of directly dated contemporary outliers, with extra Central Steppe-, Yamnaya- and East European hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, indicating a cosmopolitan site.
evidence.location: Results, Inner Asian Mountain Corridor section; Fig. 2

evidence.claim: Individuals from Krasnoyarsk dated about 1700-1500 BCE derive up to about 25% of their ancestry from an East Asian-related source with the rest Western_Steppe_MLBA, and by the Late Bronze Age East Asian-related admixture was ubiquitous in the Kazakh steppe transect.

East of the Urals from about 3,700 years ago, steppe-related ancestry peaks at about 70% in the earliest individuals then decays, and is correlated with Globular Amphora-related farmer ancestry, consistent with eastward expansion of admixed western steppe pastoralists of the Sintashta and Andronovo complexes.

Three Copper Age Botai individuals (about 3500-3300 BCE, northern Kazakhstan) were sequenced, one at 13.6x coverage and two at lower coverage; the earliest unambiguous evidence for horse husbandry comes from Botai, around 3500-3000 BCE.

Coalescent modelling places Botai, central steppe and Okunevo groups as deeply separated from other ancient and present-day populations, best fitted as mixtures of ancient North Eurasian (ANE) ancestry and an Ancient East Asian component, with mixing dated to around 5000 BCE.
evidence.note: momi model; dating approximate.

evidence.claim: Botai show no sign of Caucasus hunter-gatherer ancestry, which Yamnaya carry; the model suggests the Botai and Yamnaya lineages diverged about 15,000 years ago, with gene flow between them not significantly different from zero.
The two male Botai individuals carry Y haplogroups N (basal) and R1b1a1, neither of which is found in Yamnaya males, who carry other R1b lineages.

Central Asia shows continuity from the Upper Paleolithic to the end of the Copper Age; Paleolithic-descended hunter-gatherers persisted largely isolated after the Yamnaya and Afanasievo expansions, and the authors favour horse domestication by hunter-gatherers, although some propose Botai learned it from western pastoralists.

The petrous part of the temporal bone, the densest bone in the body, which houses the inner ear, is the only skeletal element shown systematically to give a higher share of endogenous DNA than other elements; most fossil specimens hold about 1% endogenous DNA or less, with exceptions.
Across ten petrous bones, the dense inner-ear bone (otic capsule) gave endogenous DNA shares up to 65 times those of the surrounding dense petrous bone and up to 177 times those of the spongy apex.

Temperate-region petrous bones gave 35-70% human reads from the inner-ear part, whereas the five bones from hot regions gave under 1% from every part; the authors stress the importance of the burial environment.

Bone preparation took place in a dedicated room by researchers wearing full-cover suits, double gloves, hair nets and face masks; tools and surfaces were cleaned with a DNA-decontamination solution and ethanol and then UV-irradiated; each bone part was UV-irradiated for 10 minutes per side.
evidence.location: Methods: Selection of sampling parts within the petrous bone

evidence.claim: Negative controls were included at one per five samples for grinding, extraction, library preparation and indexing PCR.
evidence.location: Methods: DNA extraction, library preparation and sequencing

evidence.claim: For well-preserved temperate bones, the authors conclude that a low-milligram amount of the inner-ear bone holds enough endogenous DNA for multifold coverage of the nuclear genome, so choosing the right part of the bone matters more than the amount.

One protocol digested about 150 mg of powder in a buffer with EDTA, detergent and proteinase K for 24 hours at 55 C and then 24 hours at 37 C; undissolved bone was spun down and the liquid kept for purification.
evidence.location: Methods: DNA extraction, library preparation and sequencing

evidence.claim: The inner petrous bone and tooth-root cementum are recognised as the best substrates for ancient human genomics; in paired samples from the same skulls, average endogenous DNA was 40.0% for petrous bone and 16.4% for tooth cementum, and skull-vault (parietal) bone averaged about 2-3%.
evidence.note: Parietal average given as 2.2% in the Abstract and 2.8% (nine skeletons) in Results.

evidence.claim: Teeth with good molecular preservation (over 10% endogenous DNA) matched their paired petrous bones on average, while poorly preserved teeth were clearly outperformed by petrous bone.
Endogenous DNA content in ancient samples is often below 1% because DNA degrades over time and microbes invade skeletal tissue.
Seven petrous bones from cremated skeletons held under 0.03% endogenous DNA and no sign of authentic ancient human DNA.
evidence.location: Results: Endogenous DNA; Discussion: Cremated petrous bones

evidence.claim: In this lab's protocol, crushed samples were dissolved in a digestion buffer of EDTA with proteinase K for 24 hours at 37 C, and DNA was purified on silica with a binding buffer efficient for short fragments.

Because shotgun sequencing reads molecules indiscriminately, the endogenous share largely sets the cost; petrous bone and cementum gave about 8 times the endogenous share of parietal bone, roughly an 8x genome for the price of 1x.
Reads were mapped to the hg19 human reference, duplicates were removed, and endogenous content was computed as mapped human reads divided by reads kept after trimming.

Mitochondrial-to-nuclear coverage ratios averaged 157 in well-preserved teeth and 79 in the paired petrous bones, showing many more mitochondrial than nuclear copies.
Standard ancient DNA sampling destroys material by drilling or cutting and powdering parts of bones and teeth, and concern about destructive sampling has grown with the field.

Published protocols that reduce destruction of the petrous bone include sampling the inner-ear ossicles and targeted drilling of the cochlea through the cranial base of complete or reconstructed skulls.

evidence.claim: In a minimally destructive method, the tooth root is wrapped in parafilm except for a targeted lower part, which is soaked in EDTA and proteinase K extraction buffer for 2.5 hours at 37 C; there is no drilling or grinding, and the tooth remains suitable for most morphological study and for radiocarbon dating.
In paired roots, the soaked root gave on average 35.8% endogenous molecules versus 18.8% for a powdered whole root, with no significant difference in library complexity.

Petrous samples gave more complex DNA (more unique molecules) than cementum by one metric, and the authors say petrous sampling remains justified when preservation is poor; the method was tested mainly on well-preserved teeth, and friable roots crumbled.

Standard protocols remove the outer surface of bone or tooth with a sanding disc or sandblaster; the minimally destructive method instead wiped the tooth with 2% bleach, rinsed it with 95% ethanol and UV-irradiated it for 5-10 minutes per side, with contamination similar to destructive methods.
All work was done in dedicated clean rooms, and a negative control (extraction buffer in an empty tube) was processed with every extraction batch.
About 50 mg of powder was taken from each petrous bone; robotic extractions used about 37 mg of powder and manual extractions up to 50 mg.
Powders were incubated for about 18 hours (overnight) at 37 C in 0.45 M EDTA with proteinase K, and DNA was then bound to silica spin columns following Dabney et al. 2013, or extracted robotically.
Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 500 with 2x76 or 2x101 cycles; adapters were trimmed and read pairs merged requiring a 15 bp overlap.

evidence.claim: Merged reads were mapped to hg19 with BWA, chosen for consistency with most published ancient DNA; duplicates were reads sharing start, end, orientation and barcode, and only the best copy was kept.

Authenticity was assessed from mitochondrial match to consensus, autosomal contamination from linkage disequilibrium, X-chromosome contamination in males, the terminal C-to-T rate and read lengths; authentic ancient DNA has very few reads longer than 100 bp.

evidence.claim: A minimum of 95% match to the mitochondrial consensus sequence is typically applied when screening ancient DNA for population-genetic studies.

Partial UDG treatment (double-stranded libraries) or USER treatment (single-stranded libraries) removed damage inside molecules but kept it at the ends for authentication; libraries with under 3% terminal C-to-T were treated as failing screening.

evidence.claim: In the widely used earlier silica method, an extraction buffer of EDTA and proteinase K releases DNA from bone powder, which is then bound to silica with a salt-containing binding buffer, washed with an ethanol buffer and eluted in a low-salt buffer.

evidence.claim: Tested with synthetic DNA, recovery by the earlier silica method fell with length, from 72% at 150 bp to 22% at 35 bp.
A new binding buffer used in larger volume with silica spin columns recovered fragments of about 30 bp and longer efficiently.
The number of DNA fragments in an ancient sample is expected to rise steeply as length falls, so much of the information sits in very short molecules.
Library methods add priming sites by attaching adapters to molecule ends, so even very short fragments can be sequenced in full and their damage patterns used to check authenticity.
Common double-stranded library methods include a size-selective clean-up where short molecules are expected to be lost; the single-stranded method lacks this step and recovered more short sequences.
DNA fragmentation after death is at least partly driven by depurination.
Full-length molecule sequences were built by merging overlapping forward and reverse reads; unmerged reads were discarded.
evidence.location: Materials and Methods: Enrichment, Sequencing, and Assembly of the Mitochondrial Genome

evidence.claim: In Pleistocene specimens sequenced directly, most retrieved sequences came from microorganisms that colonised the tissue after death, with only a fraction from the organism itself.
The DNA letters A and G (purines) are overrepresented just before strand breaks, suggesting that depurination, after which the strand is prone to break, contributed to fragmentation.
evidence.location: Abstract; Results and Discussion: Ancient DNA Fragmentation

evidence.claim: C-to-T substitutions are greatly elevated and concentrated at the 5-prime ends of ancient molecules, with a matching G-to-A excess at 3-prime ends in a double-stranded library protocol; other substitutions are rare.

evidence.claim: Modelling indicates that cytosine deamination is far faster in single-stranded overhangs at molecule ends (an estimated 68% of cytosines there) than in double-stranded parts (about 1%).

evidence.claim: The authors argue that all steps up to adapter ligation should be done in a laboratory dedicated to ancient DNA, with project-specific adapters so that contamination from other sources and libraries can be detected.

evidence.claim: The authors argued at the time that neither fragment length nor damage-type substitutions efficiently separate endogenous from contaminating DNA, because contaminants can also be short and carry similar changes.

evidence.note: Earlier position; later work (Sawyer et al. 2012; Skoglund et al. 2014) uses damage to separate ancient from recent DNA.

evidence.claim: Most damage-derived errors in ancient DNA come from hydrolytic deamination of cytosine to uracil, which appears as C-to-T (or, on the other strand, G-to-A) differences.
Uracil-DNA glycosylase (UDG) removes uracils and leaves abasic sites, which endonuclease VIII cuts so that the shortened molecule can still enter the library.
evidence.location: Results: A UDG/endoVIII repair scheme; Fig 1

evidence.claim: In an untreated Neandertal library, C-to-T and G-to-A differences reached 40-50% at fragment ends; UDG and endonuclease VIII drastically reduced them, cutting the mitochondrial error rate from 2.20% to 0.40% per base.
evidence.location: Results: Repair of Neandertal DNA; Neandertal DNA sequence accuracy; Figs 4 and 6

evidence.claim: Reading both ends of each molecule and merging the pair (at least 11 overlapping bases) improves accuracy because Illumina accuracy drops toward the end of each read; pairs that could not be merged were discarded.
evidence.location: Results: Repair of Neandertal DNA; Neandertal DNA sequence accuracy

evidence.claim: Amplified libraries sequenced deeply contain several copies of each original molecule, recognisable by their orientation and start and end points.
Without uracil removal, true C/T or G/A heterozygous sites are hard to tell apart from deamination at low coverage, risking false heterozygote calls.
Outside permafrost, endogenous DNA in ancient remains is usually present in small amounts alongside much larger amounts of DNA from microbes that colonised the specimen after death.

Across samples from 18 to about 60,000 years old, median fragment length did not correlate significantly with age, and some samples under 100 years old had molecules as short as much older ones; the authors infer that most fragmentation happens soon after death.

The C-to-T rate at the first 5-prime position rises strongly with age; leaving aside heated specimens, every sample under 100 years old had less than 10% and every sample over 500 years old had more than 10%.
Laboratory precautions cannot remove modern DNA already in a specimen when it arrives; heating raised C-to-T rates in some specimens and bleach may raise deamination in surviving contaminant DNA.
Present-day human DNA often contaminates ancient bones and cannot easily be told apart, by its sequence, from the DNA of ancient humans.
Despite strict laboratory precautions, many ancient human fossils already contain present-day human DNA from earlier handling.

The main diagnostic feature of ancient DNA is an excess of C-to-T differences rising toward the 5-prime end of reads, usually with a complementary G-to-A excess at the 3-prime end, attributed to deamination at single-stranded ends; unlike fragment length it tends to increase over time.
Observing the damage pattern shows that degraded DNA is present but does not prove that modern contamination is absent or low.
Scoring each read for post-mortem damage and keeping only high-scoring reads reduced simulated contamination of up to about 90-95% to negligible levels in tests.
In high-coverage data, contamination can be detected as more alleles than a chromosome's copy number allows.
Contamination from a fossil's own microenvironment mainly adds statistical noise, whereas contamination from present-day humans can strongly bias population-genetic and phylogenetic analyses.
DNA extraction and library preparation up to the set-up of the amplification step were carried out in a dedicated ancient DNA laboratory.
Ligating a unique pair of barcodes to each sample's DNA molecules removes undetected cross-contamination between samples from that step onward.
Between 50 and 75 mg of bone powder was used per extraction, following Dabney et al. 2013; each sample has to be mechanically pulverised in clean conditions.

Libraries are often treated with UDG, which removes uracils, and endonuclease VIII, which cuts at the resulting abasic sites, lowering ancient-DNA errors; untreated libraries remain useful for contaminated samples.

Partial UDG treatment removes uracils inside molecules but keeps a substantial share at the terminal base (on average about 27% falling to 9%, with second-position damage about 26-fold lower), so one library serves both to test authenticity and for population genetics.

The authors propose a terminal C-to-T rate of at least 3% as the authenticity threshold for partially UDG-treated libraries, scaled down from the 10% threshold suggested for untreated libraries; it is based on one region and a 3,000-9,000-year range and may need revision.
Hybridisation capture is a standard tool because, for many ancient samples, much of the DNA in a library is not from the individual and only part of the genome is of interest.
Sample indexes added by PCR let libraries and experiments be pooled for sequencing and separated afterwards by index.
Libraries were sequenced paired-end with 2x75 or 2x150 cycles; adapters were trimmed and read pairs merged requiring at least 15 bp of overlap.

Library preparation attaches synthetic adapters to the ends of DNA molecules so they can be amplified and the sequencing reaction primed; current machines sequence millions or billions of fragments in parallel.
Single-stranded methods convert each strand of a fragment separately, doubling the chance that at least one strand is recovered and making molecules with single-strand breaks usable.
Compared with the best double-stranded method, single-stranded preparation gave on average 11.6 times more informative sequence from ancient DNA extracts and a higher share of mapped sequences.

evidence.claim: Double-stranded methods join adapters to blunt-ended double-stranded fragments; in a widely used one about half the molecules get identical adapters and cannot be sequenced, though the method is robust and inexpensive; an Illumina-type double-stranded method needs a size-selective clean-up and lost short molecules.
evidence.location: Results: A comparison of library preparation methods

evidence.claim: Single-stranded preparation remains more time-consuming than double-stranded methods, which has limited its use, and many ancient DNA studies still use the cheaper, simpler double-stranded methods.
Most sequences in ancient bone libraries were microbial; the authors describe microbial DNA as the dominant source of DNA in most ancient bones.
DNA was extracted from 50-68 mg of bone powder using the Dabney et al. silica method.

When short molecules such as fossil DNA are sequenced, reads run into adapter sequence that must be trimmed; overlapping read pairs can be merged to reconstruct the whole original molecule with better accuracy, which is especially useful for ancient DNA.
The 1240k capture uses in-solution hybridisation with synthesised probes to enrich 1,237,207 SNPs, combining sets of 394,577 and 842,630 SNPs.

evidence.claim: The 1240k capture gives genome-wide data from samples with small fractions of human DNA; median coverage on analysed SNPs was about 4 times that of a large shotgun study, from 36 times fewer reads per sample.

evidence.claim: Samples were removed for too few SNPs covered, mitochondrial evidence of contamination, X-chromosome heterozygosity in males, or an atypical X-to-Y ratio; sex was determined from the ratio of reads on the sex chromosomes.

evidence.claim: Ancient samples are represented by randomly sampled alleles rather than diploid genotypes, and statistics were computed with options that account for this.
Of more than 3,000 ancient individuals with genome-wide data published by the authors' laboratory by the end of 2021, about half had less than 10% human DNA.
evidence.location: Introduction; Methods: Estimated fraction of published ancient human genomes with <10% endogenous DNA

evidence.claim: In in-solution enrichment, synthetic DNA baits pair with complementary target molecules in a library so that other molecules can be washed away and the bound ones isolated and sequenced.

Worked example: in a library that is 1% human, about 1 in 10,000 sequences overlaps one of about 600,000 target SNPs, so 400 million shotgun reads give at most about 40,000 SNPs, while 25 million reads after enrichment can cover nearly all targets.

The 1240k reagent targets slightly fewer than 1.24 million SNPs; first used in data published in 2015, by October 2022 it had produced over 70% of genome-wide ancient human data sets, and in-solution enrichment makes samples with little human DNA economical to study.

The 1240k reagent enriches targets unevenly and favours some alleles over others, complicating co-analysis with shotgun data; the Twist Ancient DNA assay released in 2021 showed the least allelic bias of three assays tested.
Read pairs were merged, mapped to hg19 (described as the de facto standard in ancient DNA), PCR duplicates removed, and one random sequence chosen at each position for genotype calls.
Contamination can enter ancient DNA data during excavation and storage of skeletal material and during laboratory processing.

Mitochondrial sequences are almost always uniform within an uncontaminated individual, the basis of mitochondrial contamination tests, but such estimates can be biased because the ratio of mitochondrial to nuclear DNA varies by orders of magnitude between samples; estimates from apparent X-chromosome variation in males are more reliable but do not work for females.

ContamLD estimates autosomal contamination from the breakdown of linkage disequilibrium (correlations between nearby variants) caused by contaminating DNA; it works for males and females, and the authors recommend removing or explicitly modelling samples above 5% contamination.
Keeping only damaged sequences discards most authentic sequences and cannot separate authentic DNA from contamination by another ancient individual whose DNA is also damaged.

Microbial DNA often makes up the bulk of DNA from ancient human remains; bacterial sequences usually do not align to the human reference genome, but contaminating DNA from present-day people does, alongside the endogenous fragments.
One method uses deamination patterns and fragment lengths to estimate present-day human contamination in mitochondrial data and to reconstruct the ancient individual's own mitochondrial genome.

In most prehistoric skeletons, post-mortem decay leaves under 0.5% endogenous human DNA in most parts of the skeleton, the rest being mostly DNA from bacteria and fungi that colonised the body after death.

All work before amplification took place in clean rooms; bone was sampled with a sterile dentistry drill, 30-160 mg was used per extraction, negative extraction controls were included, and each library carried a sample-unique tag combination.

evidence.claim: Genetic sex can be assigned from Rx, the normalised ratio of reads on the X chromosome to reads on the autosomes: about 0.5 for males and 1.0 for females; it worked down to about 1,000 reads, whereas an earlier ratio method needs about 100,000 mapped reads.
Read pairs overlapping by 11 or more bases were merged before mapping to hg19.

The AADR reprocesses each individual's data to sequences aligned to hg19 and produces genotypes at about 1.23 million SNPs; for most individuals these are pseudo-haploid (one randomly sampled sequence per position), with diploid genotypes released where coverage allows.

disagreements.topic: When did the main Neandertal admixture happen?
disagreements.summary: Estimates range from 37,000–86,000 years ago (linkage disequilibrium in present-day genomes) to 45,000–49,000 years ago (anchored by a ~45,000-year-old genome). Recent estimates that use early ancient genomes cluster around 50,000–45,000 years ago.

disagreements.topic: How much Neandertal ancestry do non-Africans carry?
disagreements.summary: Estimates differ with the reference Neandertal genome and method: 1.5–2.1% with the Altai genome, 1.8–2.6% with the closer Vindija genome, about 2.3% in a demographic model.

All models combine southern (Caucasus/Near Eastern-related) and northern (eastern European hunter-gatherer-related) ancestry, but they differ in the sources and routes: EHG plus a Near Eastern-related population; a large CHG-related or Iranian farmer-related contribution; a contribution from Middle Don hunter-gatherers; or about four-fifths Caucasus–Lower Volga-related ancestry plus Ukraine Neolithic hunter-gatherer-related ancestry via Serednii Stih-related groups.

disagreements.topic: Did early Iranian farmers spread east into South Asia?
disagreements.summary: One study describes ancestry related to early Iranian farmers spreading east into South Asia. Later work with an Indus Valley Civilization genome finds that the Iranian-related ancestry in the Indus Periphery split before the lineage of Zagros farmers, which argues against a spread of western Iranian farmers.

positions.label: earlier-splitting Iranian-related lineage; no farmer spread

disagreements.topic: Which cluster do the Goyet Gravettian individuals belong to?
disagreements.summary: Fu et al. 2016 grouped Gravettian-associated individuals from Goyet with the Věstonice cluster; Posth et al. 2023 find them genetically intermediate between the Věstonice and Fournol clusters. They are left unassigned here.

disagreements.topic: When did people first enter the Americas?
disagreements.summary: Genetic models differ: a single founding wave no earlier than 23,000 years ago, or a founding population that split from East Asians about 36,000 years ago with a long period of structure in Beringia. Footprints at White Sands dated about 23,000–21,000 years ago place people in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum; their dating has been debated.

positions.label: founding wave no earlier than 23 ka
split from East Asians ~36 ka; Beringian structure

disagreements.topic: Where does the Australasian-related signal in some Native Americans come from?
disagreements.summary: One study attributes it to an additional founding population ('Population Y'); another attributes distant Australo-Melanesian sharing to later gene flow. The source population is unsampled.

disagreements.topic: How did Levant-related ancestry reach eastern African herders?
disagreements.summary: The Levant-related ancestry of early eastern African herders could reflect migration from the Levant or a shared ancestral population that lived earlier in Africa or the Near East; the study that reports it offers both explanations.

disagreements.topic: How did Papuan-related ancestry arrive in Vanuatu?
disagreements.summary: Studies agree that Papuan-related ancestry arrived soon after first settlement and came to dominate. They differ in timing (by ~2,300 vs from ~2,500 years ago) and in emphasis: one large movement, or repeated, incremental, sex-biased admixture.
